State Secretaries of Animal Husbandry was held regarding 
preparedness in case of outbreak of the disease.

disease intelligence. Samples so far tested at High Security Animal 
Disease Laboratory (HSADL), Bhopal were found negative. 
Training has been imparted to the staff of the State Wildlife and the 
Animal Husbandry Dapartment, how  to collect and dispatch the 
samples to the laboratory for testing. 
• There is a total ban in place agai snt import of poultry and poultry 
related products from all countries affected with bird flu outbreak. 
Even birds [grand parent stock of poultry etc.] imported from highly 
pathogenic avian influenza free countries are subjected to quarantine 
and screening.

situation. A National Consultation Meeting on Pandemic 
Preparedness was held 1st August, 2005 with all stakeholders to 
finalize pandemic preparedness and Response Plan.

has been finalized detailing immediate action to be taken to deal

discussed with the State Govts.

of bio-safety labs, personal protective equipments, stockpiling of 
drugs and Information Education Communication are being taken up

chairmanship of Secretary (H&FW) to ensure availability of drugs, 
vaccines and all other aspects for management of Avian influenza in 
the country. 
• National Institute of Communizable Diseases has been identified as 
the nodal agency for monitoring Avian Influenza and for 
investigating outbreaks. Under the aegis of ICMR, an Human 
Influenza surveillance network has been operationalized.

education 
1163. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether he is aware that the owners  of most of the private sector 
hospitals and medical colleges are essentially business men and they have 
reduced medical care to the level of a business or industry by employing over 
investigation, and performing surgery unnecessarily, keeping brain dead cases 
on ventilator for days purely for monetary gains; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that commercialisation of medical education 
has resulted into commercialisation of medical practice and ethical standards 
have fallen and the practice of medicine has become a trade but not a calling;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) 
Health being a State subject, it is  for the State Government to 
regulate/monitor the functioning of its hospitals, including private hospitals as 
well as to ensure that they comply with the norms/regulations prescribed by 
respective State Governments as well as  to take punitive action against 
private hospitals/ doctors in cases of proven unethical and unscrupulous 
conduct. In cases of over investigations , unnecessary surgeries, keeping brain 
dead cases on ventilator etc., the aggrieved party can also take recourse to 
legal remedies under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 which covers the 
private hospitals/private medical practitioners. 
166 

[2 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
In addition, the Indian Medical Counc il (Professional Conduct, Etiquette 
& Ethics) Regulations, 2002, complaints with regard to professional 
misconduct can be brought before the Medical Council of India or the 
concerned State Medical Council, as the the case may be, for disciplinary 
action. If found guilty, appropriat e Medical Council may award such 
punishment as deemed necessary or may direct the removal altogether or for 
a specified period the name of the delinquent from the register of registered 
medical practitioners. 
The National Health Policy, 2002 en visages the participation of the 
private sector in all areas of health activities—primary, seco ndary or tertiary. 
" According to the judgement dated 31st October, 2002 given by Supreme 
Court of India in the case of T.M.A. Pai Foundation & Others, v/s State of 
karnataka and others, the unaided private institutions have to adopt a rational 
fee structure and they are expected not to charge cap itation fee or indulge in 
profiteering. 
A Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court has further laid down that 
private medical institutes have the freedom to fix their own fee structure. 
However, each State Government is required to set up a Committee under the 
Chairmanship of a retired High Cour t Judge to decide whether the fee 
proposed by the institute is justified and does not amount to profiteering or 
charging of capitation fee. The said Committee may approve the fee structure 
proposed by the Institute or may propose some other fee which shall be 
binding on the institute for a period of three years. 
Junk food habit among the people 
1164. SHRI VARINDEB SINGH BAJWA:  
          SHRI DARA SINGH: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether government are aware that junk food is fast gaining popularity 
in metropolitan cities like Mumbai, Chandigarh and Delhi wherein people 
are getting quickly attracted towardsit; 
(b) if so, whether the food experts the world over, have expressed their 
concern over increasing consumption of junk food as a large number of 
children and youth far failing victims; 
(c) if so, whether Government propose to take concrete steps to check the 
expanding junk food culture in order to save our children from its adverse 
impact; 
167 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
(d) if so, by when; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (e) 
There is no specific definition for junk food. The phrase 'Junk food' is used to 
denote such food which have high level of calories and have little enzyme 
producing vitamins and minerals. When such food is consumed, the body is 
required to produce its own enzymes to convert these empty calories into 
usable energy. This is not desireable as this enzymes producing function in 
human body should be reserved for the performance of vital metabolic 
reactions. 
There is an increasing trend particularly among school children and 
adolescent population to consume 'Junk fo od' which is rich in calories but 
low in nutritive value. However, there is no large scale data on the extent of 
consumption of junk foods.  . 
There is a concerned world over regarding consumption of highly 
refined foods with only energy and little or no vitamins and minerals. 
There are studies to indicate that  there is a positive correlation 
between consumption of foods with empty calories and chronic degenerative 
diseases as well as hypertension, ob esity, cardio vascular problems and 
glucose intolerance. A study conducted by All India Institute of Medical 
Sciences (AIIMS) - Department of Science & Technology (DST) in 2002 
found that the consumption of junk food is increasing in schools and 
adolescent population. The same study has shown that this trend and 
associated life style factors in urban adolescent and young adult population 
has resulted in increase of non-co mmunicable disease among the young 
population. 
The need for education of general public to avoid junk food has 
increased and efforts are being made by Government, nutritionsts and 
dieticians to make people aware of its harmful effects. The Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare has also  prepared IEC material advising 
avoidance of junk food by all age groups of the population. These materials 
have been circulated to all the States  and are also displayed and distributed 
during 'health melas' organized by this Ministry. The National Institute of 
Nutrition (NIN) has developed dietary guidelines for Indians, where it has 
been suggested that ready to eat should be consumed judiciously and "free 
sugar" should be used sparingly.

WHO report on flu pandemic 
1166. DR. M.A.M. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the World Health Organisation has warned an outbreak of flu 
pandemic which may cause heavy damage to human lives; 
(b) if so, when the last time flu  pandemic attacked the number of human 
lives lost; 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
(c) the steps taken by Government to combat the outbreak of all kinds of 
flu, be it avain flu or human flu; and 
(d) the names of pharmaceutical companies which have started working on 
drugs to fight avain flu or human flu? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) 
World Health Organisation (WHO) has is sued an alert that Bird Flu could 
spread to India and other countries from  the very first time that the current 
outbreak of Avian Influenza Virus (H5N1) was first detected in the Republic 
of Korea in December, 2003. 
The H5N1 virus may undergo a genetic change, either mixing with 
existing human influenza strain or mutating of its own, giving rise to a 
pandemic strain to which human population has no immunity, giving rise to a 
pandemic. 
An estimated 40-50 million deaths occurred in the influenza pandemic of 
1918-1919. The pandemics of 1957 and 1968 respectively were caused by 
the milder virus, each killed 1 to 4 million people. 
No case of Bird Flu (Avian influenza) has been reported in India either in 
humans or birds in the current outbreak. 
However, Government of India took adequate measures to prevent entry 
of Avian Influenza in to India and to contain the disease if it has to happen in 
poultry or humans. The measures instituted are: 
* A Joint Monitoring Group under the Chairmanship of Director 
General 
of Health Services consisting members from Indian Council of Medical 
Research, National Institute of Communicable Diseases, World Health 
Organization and Department of Animal Husbandry is monitoring the 
situation ever since the WHO alerted the global community and advising 
appropriate actions to the Government. 
* The Department of Animal Husbandry, Dairying & Fisheries has 
prepared and circulated an Action Plan for State Animal Husbandry 
Departments in respect of Bird Flu for taking action in case of suspicion of 
outbreak of the disease and also in the event of outbreak of Highly 
Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI). A co nference of the State Secretaries of 
Animal Husbandry was held regarding preparedness in case of outbreak of 
the disease. 
* Department of Animal Husbandry has intensified surveillance and 
disease intelligence Samples so far tested at High Security Animal Disease 
172 

[2 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Laboratory (HSADL), Bhopal were found negative. Training has been 
imparted to the staff of the Stat e Wildlife and the Animal Husbandry 
Department, how to collect and dispatch the samples to the laboratory for 
testing. 
* There is a total ban in place against import of poultry and poultry related 
products from all countries affected with bird flu outbreak. Even birds [grand 
parent stock of poultry etc.] imported from highly pathogenic avian influenza 
free countries are subjected to quarantine and screening. 
* Department of Environment and Forests has issued instructions to all 
their Wild Life Wardens to keep a watch on death of migratory birds in 
identified water bodies. Any unusual death among migratory birds would 
immediately be brought to the notice of Dept. of Animal Husbandry. 
* Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is regularly reviewing the 
situation. A National Consultation Meeting on Pandemic Preparedness was 
held on 1st August, 2005 with all stakeholders to finalize pandemic 
preparedness and Response Plan. 
*A contingency plan for managing human cases of avian influenza has 
been finalized detailing immediate action to be taken to deal with any 
suspected outbreak. The state level actio n plan has been discussed with the 
State Govt. personal protective eq uipments, stockpiling of drugs and 
Information Education Communication are being taken up in a phased 
manner. 
* An Inter Ministerial Task Force has been constituted under the 
Chairmanship of Secretary (H&FW) to ensure availability of drugs, vaccines 
and all other aspects for management of Avian influenza in the country. 
* National Institute of Communicable Diseases has been identified as the 
nodal agency for monitoring Avian Influenza and for investigating outbreaks. 
Under the aegis of ICMR, and Human Influenza surveillance network has 
been operationalized. 
* The situation has also been reviewed  by Committee of Secretaries on a 
monthly basis and Ministry of Home Affairs. 
* There is no definitive treatment for human cases of avian influenza of a 
pandemic caused by a pandemic influe nza strain. Antiviral  drugs such as 
Oseltamivir, Zanamivir, Amantidine and Remantidine reduces viral load and 
improves the clinical outcome if given early. It is not known which drug 
would be effective for a pandemic stra in. For treatment of human cases of 
Avian Influenza Oseltamirvir is recommended.-M/s Roche of Switzerland

already manufactures the drug Osejtamivir (Tamiflu). Indian companies who 
have started working on the drug are M/s Cipla, M/s Hetero Drugs and M/s 
Ranbaxy.

Preventive mechanism for exploitation of the poor for clinical trials 
1168. SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT : Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) what regulatory mechanism Government have set up to prevent the 
exploitation of poor people who voluntarily go for clinical trials; 
(b) in the context of many of the volunteers being uneducated persons, 
what are the guarantees that principle of informed consent is being followed; 
and 
(c) in view of the dangers, whether Go vernment are thinking of canceling 
the January, 2005 amendment to Schedule "Y" of the Drugs and Cosmetics 
Act? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) 
Detailed norms for conducting clinical trials on a new drug in the country are 
prescribed under Drugs & Cosmetics Rules 122-DA-122-E and also under 
Schedule Y to these rules. The clinical trial shall be initiated only after the 
permission from DCG(I) and approval from respective Ethics Committee is 
obtained. 
Schedule-Y prescribes the requirements for permission to conduct clinical 
trials and/or manufacture or import of New Drugs for marketing in India. It 
also lays down safety and ethical as pects, responsibilities of sponsors, 
investigators and Institutional Ethics Committee etc. Modalities for 
obtaining informed consent from trial subjects, and a specific form for the 
same have also been prescribed. During and following a subject's 
Participation in a trial, th e investigator has to ensure that adequate medical 
care is provided to participant for any adverse event. 
The Government has brought out detailed guidelines on Good Clinical 
Practices and Indian Council of Me dical Research (ICMR) had published 
Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Re search on Human Subjects, which are 
required to be followed during conduct of a trial. 
These norms prescribed in India, are at par with international practices 
including that of U.S.A. Thus at present there is no requirement for canceling 
of the January 2005 amendment to Schedule-Y of Drugs & Cosmetics Act.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) No general ban has been imposed on booking of parcel 
consignments weighing more than 20 kgs. Parcels of any quantity can be 
booked by rail subject to availability  of accommodation in train. However, 
any package weighing more than 20 kgs. are not accepted for booking as 
parcel traffic by any train, when it is clubbed and packed together w.e.f. 
1.7.2005. Perishable parcel traffic and single item package weighing more 
than 20 kgs. were exempted from this order. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. With a view to streamline loading, East Coast 
Railway has imposed ban to avoid booking of heavy consignments. The 
main reasons for rationalisation are as under:—  
Merchants generally club many items to make a big package. Such a big 
and heavy package need three/ four persons to handle a single package. When 
number of heavy packages are many, train suffers detention for 
loading/unloading. 
Causes haphazard loading within th e Brakevan. Shelf space of the 
Brakevan remains unutilized. 
Causes jamming of passage and Brakevan door. 
Makes the packages dumped below or behind heavy packages untraceable 
at the enroute unloading points. 
Causes over carriage of parcels. 
Causes damage due to rough handling and delays in transit. 
The handling of too many heavy packages causes stress to the labourers. 
In view of the above, East Coast Railway has decided to reduce the weight 
of packages offered for booking as parcel traffic. The reduction in the number 
of heavy packages would make geographical stacking, utilization of shelf 
space, easier loading/unloading possibility  which would benefit the business 
and the railways. More parcels will reach their destination in time with less 
chances of damage. 
(d) The difficulties faced by merchants,  were taken into consideration in a 
review meeting taken by East Coast Railway and the limit of parcels has been 
increased from-20 kgs. to 30 kgs. w.e.f. 5.08.2005. This has been

Vigilant Monitoring System during heavy rains 
1177. SHRI NANDI YELL AIAH: Will the Minister  of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether in the midst of heavy rains and over-flooding of rivulets near 
culverts and railway bridges, there is any vigilant monitoring system through 
co-ordination of railway engineers and the concerned State's mandal-wise 
engineers and revenue authorities, to fore -see the dangers of railway track in 
advance; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the details of various measures alr eady in force to send messages to 
the engine driver to stop or slow down, when there is a danger to the railway 
track during the normal times and during the period of heavy rains? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) to (d) There are certain works carried out in the states 
like Irrigation Tanks and Water Reservoirs, Canals in embankments 
Marginal Bunds etc. which affect the safety of railway tracks and bridges. 
Such works are called 'Railway Affec ting Works'. It wa s therefore found 
necessary that Railway authorities are kept informed of the broad details and 
maintenance and upkeep of these works by the authorities concerned so that 
steps to ensure safety of track etc., if  necessary, could be taken in time. The 
attention of the Chief Ministers of States was drawn to the above during 
conference of chief Ministers with the Railway Minister in 5th June, 1957. It 
was decided to have State Committee of Engineers in each State consisting 
of officials from the Public Works Deptt., Irrigation, Revenue, Forest etc. of 
the States concerned and the Railway s. The State Committee of Engineers 
identify the Railway Affecting Works in  the State and also address various 
coordination issues. Government also had appointed a Committee of 
Engineers in 1967 under the Chairmanship of Dr. A.N. Khosla to study the 
various aspects related to the safety of Railway tracks and bridges with 
respect to floods. As a follow up of the recommendations of the Khosla 
Committee, accepted by the government, rules and procedures to be followed 
for the construction, maintenance, inspection and operation of 'Railway 
Affecting Works have bee laid down in the Manual of Instructions 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
for Railway Affecting Works to be uniformally adopted all over the country. 
This manual of instruction has been circulated to all State Goverments for 
approval and adoption. 
As per the laid down procedures, the parties owning the 'Railway 
Affecting Works' should regularly inspect and maintain these works as per 
the approved procedures and schedule laid down in the manual. Any repair or 
strengthening has to be carried out by them with utmost expedition before the 
onset of monsoon. Any request from Railway administration in connection 
with strengthening, repairs and maintenance and operation of all such works 
to esure safety of Railway lines is to be attended with promptitude. As per 
the laid down procedure, in case of any apprehended danger, or actual 
damage to a 'Railway Affecting work' which might affect the safety of 
Railway lines, immediate action has to be taken by the party concerned to 
advise the Station Master and the Railway Engineer concerned so as to 
enable the Railway officials to take  immediate precautionary measures to 
ensure safety of trains. The Railway engineer and the authorities owning the 
railway Affecting works also have to arrange with local authorities/village 
head men in whose jurisdiction 'Railway Affecting Works' are situated to 
watch them during periods of heavy rains and give timely intimation to

Statement 
The salient features of the National Steel Policy 
• The NSP sets out a broad roadmap for the Indian Steel Industry in its 
journey towards reform, restructuring and globalisation. 
• The long-term goal of the NSP is that India should have a modern 
and efficient steel industry of world standards, catering to diversified 
steel demand. The focus of the policy is to achieve global 
competitiveness not only in terms of cost, quality and product-mix 
but also in terms of global benechmarks of efficiency and 
productivity. 
• In order to achieve the goal of 110 million tonnes of steel production 
by 2019-20, the NSP seeks to remove the supply-side constraints to 
the growth of this industry in an open, globally integrated and 
competive environment. 
• The NSP seeks to adopt a multi-pronged strategy to move towards 
the long-term policy goal. On the demand side, the strategy would be 
to create incremental demand through  promotional efforts, creation 
of awarencess and strengthening the delivery chain, particularly in 
rural areas. On the supply side, the strategy would be to facilitate 
creation of aditional capacity, remove procedural and policy 
bottlenecks in the availability of inputs such as iron ore and coal, 
make higher investments in R&D and encourage the creation of 
infrastructure such as roads, railways, and ports. 
• The NSP acknowledges the low per capita consumption of steel in 
the country, especially in the rura l areas and the need to boost steel 
consumption to improve quality of life and help in meeting the 
growing aspirations of masses. 
• In order to achieve the strategic goal of 110 mT of steel production 
by 20 19-20, the industry would need addtional capital. In addtion, 
funds would be required for technological upgrade of existing 
facilities. In order to mobilize such vast resources NSP seeks to 
encourage foreign direct investment. In addition the policy also 
seeks to make the fiscal incentives, available to infrastructure 
projects, accessible to the steel industry. 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2005] 
• The NSP seeks to support developi ng of risk-hedging instruments 
like futures and derivatives to contain price volatility in the steel 
market. 
• The NSP seeks to strengthen the existing training and research 
facilities available to the domestic steel industry so as to provide 
suitable training programmes especially for the secondary small-
scale units and also to collect and analyze data on important 
parameters of the industry. 
• The NSP seeks to mount aggressive R&D efforts to create 
manufacturing capability for special types of steel, substitute coking 
coal, use iron ore fines, develop new products suited to rural needs, 
enhance material and energy efficiency, utilize waste, and arrest 
environmental degradation. 
• The NSP acknowleges the important role played by the secondary 
steel sector in providing employment, meeting local demand of steel 
in rural and semi-urban areas, and meeting the country's demand of 
some special products and seeks to endeavour to provide the 
necessary feedstock to these units at reasonable prices from major 
plants through the ex isting mechanism of State Small Industries 
Corporations. 
• The NSP recognizes the fact that intergration of the Indian steel 
industry with the global economy requires that the industry should 
be protected from unfair trade practices, which become common 
especially during periods of downturn. The NS P therefore, 
envisages, institution of mechanisms for import surveillance, and 
monitoring export subsidies in other countries.

*185. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS K AUR: Will the Minister of 
PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. is contemplating a 
joint venture for setting up a new refinery in Bina and in Madhya Pradesh; 
(b) if so, the details of the joint venture; 
(c) whether a detailed design and feasibility report for the same has 
also been prepared, if so, the estimate d cost and capacity of the projected 
refinery; and 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2005] 
(d) the progress made so far in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL) have plans to set up 
a refinery at Bina (Madhya Pradesh) with crude oil import facilities at Vadinar 
(Gujarat) and a cross-country crude oil pipeline from Vadinar to Bina. 
(b) BPCL and Oman Oil Company Limi ted (OOC) had formed a Joint 
Venture named Bharat Oman Refineries Limited (BORL) on 23.12.1993 to 
set up a refinery project. According to the Joint Venture Agreement, the final 
contribution by BPCL and OOC in the equity capital of BORL was 26% each. 
Later on, OOC desired to limit its contribution to the amount already 
contributed by them. Accordingly, a supplemental agreement was signed on 
9.9.2004 limiting OOC's contribution to the tune of Rs. 75.5 crore and 
revising their rights accordingly. 
(c) A Detail Feasibility Report for the refinery project was originally 
prepared in September, 1994. However, implementation of the project got 
delayed owing to the denial of certain environmental clearances. The refinery 
configuration has since been revised, keeping in view the changed 
demand/supply scenario and future standards for gasoline and diesel oil. 
The approved cost of the 6 million metric tonne per annum capacity 
refinery project is Rs.6,354 crore (as of September, 2001 prices). 
(d) Land for the refinery block at Bi na and for the crude oil terminal 
at Vadinar have been acquired. The ac quisition of Right of User/Right of 
Way along the route of the crude oil pipeline has been completed. All 
major statutory and environmental approvals for the project have been 
received. As of October 2005, the total comulative commitment for the 
project was Rs. 243.28 crore and the cumulative expenditure was 
Rs. 165.63 crore. Physical progress of the project is 5.3%.

Shutdown by LPG producing plants 
*187. SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE:†  
          SHRI CHITTABRATA MAJUMDAR: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the details of unforeseen shutdowns in LPG producing plants in 
public and private sector refineries during last six months, month-wise; 
(b) whether a planned shutdown for 45 days was resorted to by 
Jamnagar Refinery from 4th October, 2005; 
(c) if so, its impact on LPG shortage in the country in domestic sector, and 
(d) the reason, for permitting such planned shutdown during peak demand in 
festive season? 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Dipankar 
mukherjee. 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2005] 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Due to planned and unforeseen shutdowns by refineries, there has 
been a reduction in the actual production of LPG vis-a-vis production planned 
originally during the current year. The month-wise details of production of LPG 
for the period April-October, 2005 are given in the Statement-I (See below). 
The details of shutdowns, planned and unforeseen, of various major units in 
public and private sector refineries du ring April-October, 2005 are given in 
Statement-I I (See below). 
(b) A planned shutdown for Reliance India Limited (RIL) Refinery at 
Jamnagar was taken with effect from 4th October, 2005. Production was restored 
on 1 st December, 2005. 
(c) As the Jamnagar Refinery accounts for about one-third of the domestic 
production of LPG the Reliance shutdown made it necessary to effect imports 
at just the time the international market for LPG was severely hit by hurricanes 
like Katrina, Rita and Wilmar and ONGC gas production was temporarily affected 
by the BHN fire. 
(d) While the planned shutdown of the refineries is essential for 
maintenance requirements and the safety of refinery units, and the permission 
of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas is not required for such shutdowns, 
it is a fact that the Reliance shutdown was initially planned for April-May, later 
changed to August-September and fi nally took place in October-November, 
2005. Precisely because the shutdown was eventually scheduled for the festive 
season, the Ministry proactively interacted with Reliance to further postpone 
the shutdown. Reliance pleaded that for technical reasons, it was not possible 
for them to shift the shutdown till after the festive season. Repeated 
postponements and the decision to close down at the height of the festive 
season certainly complicated matters for the OMCs as Reliance accounts 
for nearly one-third of domestic LPG production.

*181. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of TOURISM 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that perspective plans of 20 years for developing 
tourism in the States have been prepared; 
(b) if so, the details and the target of these plans; and 
(c) the details of plans envisaged in respect to Tamil Nadu? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF TOURISM 
(SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The broad objectives of the perspective plans for the States were to: 
(i) assess the existing tourism scenario in the States; 
(ii)  review the status of existing development/investment plans; 
(iii) evaluate the existing potential tourist destinations; 
(iv) develop sustainable tourism in a time period of 20 years; 
(v) identify the existing as well as new tourism projects that have 
potential for development; 
(vi) give plans with short term and long term targets; 
(vii) indicate the likely investment on infrastructure development under 
different heads; and

[6 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(viii) prepare an action plan for implementation of identified potential 
schemes/projects, and for development of infrastructure. 
(c) The twenty year perspective pl an for the State of Tamil Nadu has 
categorized various destinations in the State under six broad heads viz. 
Pilgrimage Destinations; Heritage Locations and Historical Monuments; 
Locations of Scenic Beauty (hill stati ons, beaches, and forests/sanctuaries); 
Tourist Festival Locations; Adventure Destinations; and Leisure Destinations. 
Accordingly, the plan has prioritized various projects in the State, to be taken 
up in short run and long run. 
As development of potential tourism desinations is primarily the 
responsibility of the State/UT Governments, the 20 years Perspective Plans 
were sent to the States/UTs for preparation of their developmental plans 
accordingly. 
Support and suggestions from world Bank on water related 
issues 
*183. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the World Bank has enhanced the quantum of its loan for 
water-related sectors in India from $200 million a year to $800 million a year 
for four years; 
(b) what are the pre-conditions set forth by the Bank for extending this 
loan package; 
(c) whether the World Bank report on India's performance on water-related 
issues, mentions of poor management and predicts a turbulent future, devoid 
of minimum requirement of water to sustain its economy; and 
(d) whether the Bank has recommended construction of mega 
dams in the country to enhance its  water storage capacity from the 30 
days of rainfall to 900 days as is done in major river basins in arid area 
of developed countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) The Country Director, 
World Bank has indicated an enhancement of fund allocation 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2005] 
by World Bank for water resources projects from present level of US$ 200 
million per year to about US$800 million per year. 
(b) The projects are sanctioned and governed by general terms and 
conditions that are applicable to all World Bank projects in all sectors world over. 
In so far as any specific conditions, if any, are concerned the same are discussed 
on case to case basis depending upon the projects concerned. 
(c) Mr. John Briscoe of the World Ba nk has recently prepared a draft 
Report titled "India's Water Economy: Br acing for a Turbulent Future." The 
report is based on study conducted by the World Bank on its own. The report in 
general discusses various aspects of water resources development and 
management in India and broadly covers the issues related to: 
i. adjusting to the needs of a changing India; 
ii. adjusting to scarcity and greater variability; 
iii. dealing with growing conflicts; 
iv. maintaining and renewing existing infrastructure; 
v. building infrastructure in under-served areas and for under-served 
public purposes. 
vi. making the transition from development to management and 
development; 
vii. revitalizing the machinery of Government to deal with the turbulent 
water future; and 
viii. charting a prioritized, sequenced, pragmatic path for making 
improvements. 
Most of the issues are duly addressed in the National Water Policy and 
appropriate actions are taken in light to the present policies of the Union and 
the State Governments. 
(d) The drafts reports states that  India has relatively little capacity 
to store water. It further states that whereas there is about 900 days of 
storage capacity in the Colorado and Murray Darling rivers, there is only 
about 30 days of storage capacity in  most of India's river basins and 
accordingly major investments need to  be made to increase capacity to 
store water, in both surface and groundwater reserviors, in projects small 
(such as local rainwater harvesting) and big (such as large dams).

Bio-diesel policy 
†*186. DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
          SHRI RAM JETHMALANI:  
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that bio-diesel can be prepared from Ratan Jot; 
(b) if so, whether it has been confirmed officially; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that Government have not been able to 
decide any policy regarding bio-diesel so far; and 
(d) if so, the details in this regard and by when, the policy is likely to 
be decided? 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
19 
 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2005] 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (d) Bio-diesel, a diesel fuel substitute, can 
be made from vegetable oils (both edible and non-edible) and animal fats. Studies 
have been undertaken in R&D and academic institutions to explore the 
possibility of production of bio-diesel from non-edible oils like Jatropha 
curcas (Ratan jot) and Pongamia (Karanj), and these have been found to be 
suitable feedstock for the production of bio-diesel. 
The Ministry of Rural Development is the nodal Ministry to implement 
the proposed National Mission on Bio-diesel, which inter alia, envisages 
large scale plantation of Jatropha Curcas (Ratan Jot). The Detailed Project 
Report for the proposed National Mission on Bio-diesel, which was referred 
by the Ministry of Rural Development to the Planning Commission, has not 
yet received all clearances and approvals which are a prerequisite for deciding 
upon any policy regarding bio-diesel. 
However, for providing marketing support to bio-diesel for use as 
trasnsportation fuel through blending with diesel, the Ministry of Petroleum and 
Natural Gas has issued a Statement on Bio-diesel Purchase Policy, which 
comes into effect on 1.1.2006. The policy identifies 20 purchase centres of the 
public sector oil marketing companies at which these companies will purchase 
bio-diesel which satisfies the prescribed Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) 
specifications from those bio-diesel manufacturers who get registered with the 
oil marketing companies after satisfying the technical and other credentials. 
The initial price at which the oil marketing companies will purchase bio-
diesel is Rs. 25 per litre. This prices can be reviewed by the oil marketing 
companies every six months. Depending upon felt need and preparedness, the 
oil companies could also open more purchase centres.

RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. All the 
States were requested to reassess th e ground water resources based on the 
recommendations of the Groundwater Estimation Committee (GEC) 1997. 
However, none of the States could complete ground water resource estimation 
within the stipulated time. Such estimation has since been completed by all the 
States/Union Territories. The total replenishable Annual Ground Water 
Resources of the country is assessed as 433 Billion Cubic Metres (BCM) and

ground water resources. However, following steps have been taken by the 
Union Government in this regard:—

enable them to enact suitable legislation for regulation and control 
of ground water development. Central Ground Water Authority 
(CGWA) has also notified specifi ed critical areas for regulating 
drawl of ground water. 
(ii) Steps have been taken to adopt artificial recharge and rain water 
harvesting measures which incl ude, circulation of Manual/ 
Guidelines on Artificial Recharge of Ground Water to States/Union 
Territories, implementation of a Central Sector Scheme for Study of 
Recharge to Ground Water during the VIII and IX Five Year Plans. 
(iii) Steps have been taken for creation of mass awareness on water 
conservation by holding mass awareness and training programmes on rain 
water harvesting and artificial recharge of ground water. Water 
conservation campaigns launched keeping in view the various target 
groups like youth and children, women, fanners and villagers, etc., 
publicity done through mass media etc.

Statement 
Extract of the scheme on Establishment of a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) 
for funding Infrastructure Projects 
The Scheme 
In order to implement the Budget Announcement, the Department of 
Economic Affairs has drawn up a Scheme for Financing Viable Infrastructure 
Projects through a Special Purpose Vehicl e (hereinafter referred to as the 
Scheme). 
The salient features of the Scheme are: 
(a) The Scheme will be implemented by a Special Purpose Vehicle called 
the India Infrastructure Financ ing Company Ltd. (hereinafter 
referred to as the IIFCL). The II FCL will be incorporated as a 
Company under the Companies Act, 1956. 
(b) The IIFCL would finance only commercially viable projects 
sponsored by any entity viz. Public sector, Private sector or public private 
partnerships. Viable projects may also include those projects which 
become viable after receiving viability gap funding under a 
Government scheme. 
(c) The projects may belong to the following sectors: 
(i)   Roads and bridges, railways, seaports, airports, inland waterways 
and other transportation projects, 
(ii)   Power; 
(iii)   Urban transport, water supply, sewage, solid waster management 
and other physical infrastructure in urban areas; 
(iv)   Gas pipelines; 
71 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2005] 
(v)   Infrastructure projects in Special Economic Zones; and 
(vi)   International convention centres and other tourism infrastructure 
projects. 
Provided that an Empowered Committee may, with approval of the 
Finance Minister, add or delete any s ector/ sub-sectors from this list. The 
Empowered Committee as defined in the Scheme would be a Committee 
under the Chairmanship of Secretary (Economic Affairs) and include Secretary, 
Planning Commission, Secretary (Expenditure) and Secretary of the line 
Ministry dealing with the subject. 
(d) The IIFCL may render financial assistance through one or more 
of the following means: 
(i) Direct lending to the eligible projects. Normally the IIFCL will 
lend that portion of the debt that is over ten years' maturity. 
(ii) Refinance to Banks and Financial Institutions for loans with 
tenure of five years (preferably ten years) or more. 
(iii) Any other method approved by  the Government from time to 
time. 
(e) The SPV will not undertake any appraisal of Infrastructure on 
its own. The appraisal of the project would be done by the lead 
bank of the Inter-Institutional Group (Lenders' Consortium) 
financing the project. To qualify as a lead bank for the purpose 
of this scheme, a bank must have a minimum exposure of 25% 
of total project debt. All disbursements and recoveries would be 
undertaken through the lead bank. 
(f) Loan assistance from the "SPV sh all not exceed 20% of the project 
cost. 
(g) A project awarded to a private sector company for development, 
financing, construction, maintenance and operation through Public 
Private Partnership (as defined in the Scheme for Support to Public 
Private Partnerships in Infrastructure) shall have overriding priority 
under this scheme if a project is awarded through open competitive 
bidding. 
72 

[6 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(h) Private sector companies that implement infrastructure projects, except 
as a competitively bid Public Private Partnership Project, will not be 
eligible for direct lending and only the refinancing option will be 
available in such cases. Further, the total lending to such projects will 
be kept within 20% of the lending programme of the llFCL

Statement-ll 
The steps taken by Reserve Banks of India to increase institutional finance to 
agriculture 
Following steps have been taken by Reserve Bank of India to increase 
institutional finance to agriculture: 
(a) Formulation of Special Agricultural Credit Plan (SACP) by sector banks 
since 1994. As recommended by the Advisory Committee on Flow of 
Credit to Agriculture and Related Activities from the Banking 
System (Vyas Committee) and anno unced in the Mid Term Review 
of Annual Policy for 2004-05, the SACP mechanism has been made 
applicable to private sector banks from the year 2005-06. 
(b) The Kisan Credit Card (KCC) Scheme was introduced by 
NABARD in August 1998, through which major share of crop loans 
is being routed. Since inception of the scheme, public sector banks 
have issued 1.76 crore KCCs up to March 2005. NABARD has 
since revised the scheme, which covers term credit as also working 
capital for agriculture and alli ed activities and a reasonable 
component for consumptions needs. 
(c) Several recommendations of the Vyas Committee have been accepted 
and communicated to banks for implementation. These include: waiver 
of margin/security norms for agricultural loans up to 50,000 and in 
case of agri-clinics, up to Rs. 5 lakh; inclusion of investment in 
securitized agricultural loans under priority sector; review of NPA 
norms in agriculture lending; brining about procedural simplification; 
financing of oral lessees through the SHG and Joint Liability Group 
(J,U3) approach; appointment of direct selling agents by banks; 
involvement in contract farming where legal issues have been 
addressed, etc. 
(d) The Service Area Approach (SAA) has been reviewed and, as 
announced in the mid-term review of Annual Policy Statement for 
the year 2004-05, the restrictive provisions of the scheme have been 
dispensed with. 
(e) In order to encourage banks to lend directly to the priority sector 
borrowers, the facility of treating the investment made by banks 
90 

[6 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
in special bonds issued by specified institutions (NABARD, SIDBI, 
REC, NHB, HUDCO) as their indirect lending to the priority sector is 
being phased out. 
(f) Advances granted by banks up to Rs. 5 lakh to farmers against 
pledge/hypothecation of agricultural produce including warehouse 
receipts for a period not exceeding 12 months were treated as direct 
agricultural advances under the Priority Sector. Keeping in view the 
importance of post-harvest operations, the above credit limit has been 
increased to Rs. 10 lakh.

Current SSI/tiny industries definition may continue. Units with 
investment in plant and machinery in excess of SSI limit and up to Rs. 10 
crore may be treated as Medium Enterprises Development Bill. Only SSI 
financing will be included in Priority Sector.

sector by 2009-10. 
3.2 Public Sector Banks will be advise d to follow a transparent rating 
system with cost of credit being linked to the credit rating of the 
enterprise. SME rating agency has since been set up by SIDBI.

collect and pool common data on risks in each identified cluster and

Unified Tax Regime 
1419. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the Commerce Associations have urged Government to 
initiate action towards integration of Central Value Added Tax (VAT) and 
State level VAT; and 
(b) whether it is proposed to bring a Unified Tax Regime, if so, the 
details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE 
(SHRI S.S. PALANIMANlCKAM): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b)As per the provisions of the Constitution, the Central Government is 
empowered to levy tax on manufacture of goods (CENVAT), whereas the State 
Governments have the powers to levy tax on purchase or sale of goods within a 
State (State VAT). Therefore, integration of CENVAT and State VAT would 
require a constitutional amendment. Moreover, a number of other issues would 
require to be settled, in consultation with the States, before a Unified Tax 
Regime is implemented. Some States have not implemented VAT yet. The 
Central Sales Tax on inter-State sale of goods will also need to be integrated 
with VAT. There is also the question of integration of taxation of goods and 
services. Thus, there is no prospect of implementation of a Unified Tax Regime 
in the immediate future.

(SHRI S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) and (b) The National Common 
Minimum Programme (NCMP) adopted by the Government outlines the 
policy of the Government with respect to the Public Sector, including 
disinvestment of Government's equity in Central Public Sector Enterprises

(i) The Government is committed to a strong and effective public 
sector whose social objectives are met by its commercial

existing "navratna" companies in the public sector while these 
companies raise resources from the capital market . While every 
effort will be made to modernize and restructure sick public 
sector companies and revive sick industry, chronically loss-making 
companies will either be sold-off, or closed, after all workers have

induct private industry to -turn around companies that have

Strengthening of Panchayati Raj Institutions 
1469. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILA NIA: Will the Minister of 
PANCHAYATI RAJ be pleased to state: 
(a) the status of Panchayati Raj Institutions, State-wise and the steps 
being taken to strengthen such institutions; 
(b) whether any steps have been or are being taken to determine the 
functional areas of the different tiers of  local bodies in order to strengthen 
the Panchayati Raj Institutions; 
(c) whether any steps have been or are being taken to provide them the 
staff and budget under Government to the Panchayati Raj Institutions; and 
(d) if so, the details of such steps taken as on date, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANI SHANKAR 
AIYAR): (a) to (d) All States to which the Constitution 73rd Amendment Act 
1992 applies, except Jharkhand and Pondicherry, have held elections and 
constituted Panchayats in accordance with the provisions of Part IX of the 
Constitution. However, as the Constitution provides that it is legislatures of 
States that will endow the Panchayati Raj Institutions with powers and authority, 
States have devolved powers and responsibilities to the Panchayats in varying 
measure. 
To provide an impetus to the implementation of Part IX of the 
Constitution in letter and spirit, by States, the Ministry of Panchayati Raj 
135 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2005] 
convened seven Round Tables of States Ministers in charge of Panchayati Raj 
between July and December, 2004.and evolved, by consensus, a set of around 150 
points for action, which have been put together in a compendium that was adopted 
unanimously at the conclusion of the last Round Table in Jaipur. The joint 
programme of action seeks to ensure that on the basis of Activity Mapping, Panchayats at 
various levels are devolved with funds, functions and functionaries to enable them to 
emerge as institutions of self-government. 
A Council of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj under the Chairmanship 
of the Union Minister for Panchayati Raj has been constituted to review the 
implementation of the recommendations. The first meeting of the Council was held on 
5th-6th August, 2005 at Kochi, Kerala. The progress in devolution of functions was 
reviewed and it was noted that while in some States, the preliminary work has been 
completed in terms of the assignment of functions to the three levels of Panchayats, in 
several more, the matter is pending at the finalization stage. A copy of Joint Statement of 
conclusions arrived at the meeting is at Statement (See below). A Committee of Chief 
Secretaries of States and State Panchayati Raj Secretaries has also been 
constituted under the Chairmanship of the Secretary, Ministry of Panchayati Raj to 
monitor the progress on the implementation of the 150 recommendations of the Seven 
Round Tables and the decisions of the Council of States Ministers of Panchayati Raj. Four 
review meetings of the Committee have so far been held in April, 2005, June, 2005, 
September, 2005 and November 2005. 
With a view to interacting with Panchayats and carrying out a review with the 
authorities concerned of the progress in implementing the points for action mutually agreed 
upon in the Round Tables, a process of visiting the States and UTs at the level of Union 
Minister for Panchayati Raj has been initiated. Eight States have been covered so 
far, including Karnataka, West Bengal, Uttaranchal, Haryana, Chhattisgarh, Orissa, 
Arunachal Pradesh and Rajasthan. Andhra Pradesh is next on the list. Each visit is 
concluded with a Statement of Conclusions jointly signed with the Chief Minister of the 
State concerned, highlighting the key points of action on which the State would 
move to operationalise the recommendations of the Round Tables. 
136 

[6 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
Copy of the Joint statement of Conclusions arrived at the first meeting of the 
Council of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj held at Kochi on 5 and 6 August, 2005. 
In order to operationlise the provisions of Article 243 G of the Constitution, 
which provides for devolution to empower Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) to function 
as institutions of self-government for making plans and implementing programmes for 
economic development and social justice and first Round Table of State Ministers of 
Panchayati Raj held at Kolkata in July 2004 resolved as follows, under the heading, 
"Effective Devolution of Functions". 
"the essential step is the identification of activities related to the devolved 
functions with a view to attributing each of these activities to the appropriate 
tier of the 3-tier system," (Item III), 
"On the basis of the identification of activities relating to devolved 
functions, and through the application of the principle of the subsidiarity, 
States/UTs may review/undertake time bound activity mapping with a view to 
completing this exercise within the fiscaR year 2004-05;" (Item V), 
"With a view to promoting a measure of irrevocability of devolved 
functions, devolution may be routed through legislative measures or 
alternatively, by providing a strong legislative framework for devolution 
through executive orders." (Item VIII) 
The First Meeting of the Council of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj reviewed 
the progress in this direction and noted that while in some States, the preliminary work 
has been completed in terms of the assignment of functions to the three levels of 
Pachayats, in several more, the matter is pending at the finalization stage. 
However in most States, there is a need to take several more substantive steps 
in the direction of reforms for strengthening Panchayats in the true letter and spirit of the

deliberate speed and resolved to accord priority to the specific following steps:

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2005]

devolution of functions and activities to all levels of Panchayats, 
States will expedite the issuing of necessary orders to operationalise the 
same. Copies of Government orders/ Gazette Notifications will be 
intimated to Ministry of Panchayati Raj.

take preparatory steps through dissemination of draft frameworks 
prepared to the Panchayats, so that they are in a state of preparedness

particularly with reference to their roles in planning and 
implementation. The Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj will extent 
financial and technological assistance, if asked. 
v. Particular emphasis will be give n to training and orientation of 
officials of various line departments, so that they better understand 
their role in the changed context of devolution of activities to 
Panchayats and are better equipped to assume a facilitatory role. The 
Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj will extent financial and 
technological assistance, if asked.

Activity Mapping, the Panchayats would need a matching transfer of 
funds in respect of the devolved functions. This will require the 
entrustment of all schemes pertaining to the activities devolved upon 
Panchayats to the respective levels through the creation of a 
Panchayat Sector in the State Budget, The State Ministers undertake 
to take steps in this direction, so as to meet the deadline agreed upon 
in the Kolkata Round Table to

[6 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
operationalise the transfer of schemes to Panchayats in the budget 
of 2006-07. The Union Ministry of Panchayat Raj will take into 
account progress in this regard in the administration of the Panchayat 
Empowerment Incentive Fund after this is established.

have been devolved upon them it is necessary that funds pertaining 
to these schemes are transferred to them without delay or diversion.

†1473. SHRI LALIT KISHORE CHAT URVEDI: Will the Minister of 
PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the last month's strike of transporters and reduction in market 
supply by cutting supply of LPG by gas manufacturers was sponsored; and

methods by encouraging black marketing of gas? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) Public Sector Oil Marketing 
Companies (OMCs) have reported that there was no strike by their LPG 
transporters during the months of October, 2005. 
As regards the temporary LPG shortage, it may be stated that the LPG 
requirements are met by a combination of domestic production and imports. 
A temporary shortage of LPG emerged in September, 2005 on account of 
various factors. PSU production in the period April -September, 2005 was 
303 (Thousand Metric Tonne) TMT less than planned; Reliance Industries 
Ltd. (RIL) production was 190 TMT less than planned. In consequence, 
physical inventories with oil marketing companies (OMCs) declined from 
333 TMT at the beginning of April, 2005 to 190 TMT at the beginning of 
October, 2005. Then, with effect from 4th October, 2005, RIL, the single 
largest domestic supplier of LPG, shut down their Fluidized Catalytic Cracker 
(FCC) unit at Jamnagar for maintenance work. Moreover, at just about the 
same time, as RIL confirmed its shutdo wn effective October, 2005, domestic 
production prospects were seriously empacted by the fire in Mumbai High 
North and global LPG supplies became tight, largely on account of the impact 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
142 

[6 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
of Hurricane Katrina on US refineries. All these factors put together upset the 
plans made by OMCs to effect imports in time to offset the anticipated shortage 
in supplies. This fed rumours in the market that OMCs would not be able to 
meet the demand, leading to a sudden spurt in demand. There was also a strike 
in bottling plants in the National Capital Territory (NCT) area towards the end 
of September, 2005 which aggravated the situation. 
The Ministry took matters in hand early in October, 2005 when it was 
decided that through a combination of inventory management and imports, 
directly handled by a composite task force of the OMCs under the close 
supervision of the Government, physical shortages of supply would be 
overcome as quickly as possible. It was also decided that bottling plants in 
the NCT area would work on Sunday, 9th October, 2005 and other holidays. 
On the basis of these decisions, it wa s announced that the physical shortage 
in the NCT area would end by Dusshera and substantively in the rest of the 
country by Deepavali. Th ese objectives have been largely achieved. In 
addition to the arrangements made earlier by OMCs to import 642 TMT of 
LPG during the period October-December 2005, arrangements have been 
made to import an additional quantity of 237.9 TMT during this period, 138 
TMT of which has already reached the country. Thus, the overall physical 
shortage in the country at present has been reduced to only about 1.5% of the 
average monthly consumption of LPG. However, the backlog at the micro-
level may vary from market to market on account of operational reasons. 
The production of LPG in RIL's refinery has been restored from 1st 
December, 2005 and the supply situation is expected to substantively improve 
and normalize in the coming few weeks. 
While OMCs are striving to ensure supplies to distributors in 
accordance with the registered customer strength of the distributor, the active 
cooperation of State Governments is required to cap, reduce and eventually 
eliminate the diversion of domestic LPG to the black market and unauthorized 
use which takes place on account of the wide gap between the retail price of 
LPG for domestic use and the market price for commercial LPG. The Union 
Government in the Ministry of Petroleum-and Natural Gas has alerted State 
Governments to the imperative need to curtail diversion and other malpractices 
by enforcing the control orders issued under the Essential Commodities Act, 
1955. OMCs have also 
143 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2005] 
been directed to ensure adherence to Marketing Discipline Guidelines, 2001.

1480. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have any plan to lay networks of pipelines to 
bring in gas from overseas land; 
(b) whether it is a fact that some of  the countries are obstructing the 
idea of pipeline networks; and 
(c) if so, how Government ar e going to meet the energy 
requirements of India in future in the absence of such networks? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) Yes, Sir. India is pursuing import of natural gas 
from Iran through an onland pipeline via Pakistan, and from Myanmar through 
onland pipeline via Bangladesh. India has also expressed an interest in 
participating in the Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan pipeline. 
(b) and (c) No, Sir. The Government is discussing the details of the 
Iran-Pakistan-India (IPI) Gas Pipeline Project with the Governments of Iran and 
Pakistan. These discussions are progressing satisfactorily. Two separate, 
Secretary-level Joint Working Groups (JWGs), viz., India-Pakistan JWG and 
India-Iran Special JWG (SJWG) have be en constituted for this purpose. So 
far, two meetings each of the India- Pakistan JWG and the India-Iran SJWG 
have been held. The third set of meetings is scheduled for December, 2005. 
Various technical commercial, financial, legal and related issues were 
discussed in these meetings and reviewed by the Indian and Iranian Ministers 
at their meeting in Riyadh on 19th November on the sidelines of the International 
Energy Forum Round Table Conference. The Pakistan Minister is scheduled 
to visit India after the next meeting of the India-Pakistan JWG. It is envisaged 
that the project structure and Framework Agreement for the project could be 
finalized by early next year.

(P&NG) participated in a trilateral Ministerial meeting between the Oil 
Ministers of Bangladesh, Myanmar and India. In pursuance of the trilateral Joint 
Press Statement released after that meeting, a Techno-Commercial 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2005] 
Working Committee (TCWC) of the representatives of the three countries was constituted. 
The first meeting of the TCWC was held in Yangon on 24th-25th February, 2005. The 
TCWC prepared a draft MoO to be signed by the three oil Ministers after the 
approval of their respective Governments. However, the approval of the MoU has 
been delayed on account of differences between India and Bangladesh over one 
preambular paragraph in the draft MoU. Minister (P&NG) visited Dhaka on 5th 
September, 2005 to discuss issues relating to the draft MoU. These issues continue to 
be under consideration by the Governments of Bangladesh and India even as India 
explores with Myanmar other options of importing natural gas into India from 
Myanmar. 
The Governments of Turkmenistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan have been examining 
the setting up of a transnational gas pipeline to exploit the available gas reserves in 
Turkmenistan. They have designated ADB as the lead consultant and development 
partner. India has been invited to join the project it has agreed to do so, initially as an 
'Observer'. Minister (P&NG) has been invited to the next Steering Committee Meeting, 
which is tentatively scheduled to be held in Ashgabat in January, 2006.

Rationalisation of kerosene subsidy 
1485. SHRI B.K. HARIPARASAD: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in view of short recovery from kerosene touching Rs. 13.00 a 
litre and its diversion becoming drain on Oil PSUs, Government proposed to take 
the above poverty line card holders out from the purview of subsidies; 
(b) whether such a proposal when acted upon will effect in a saving of 41.2 per 
cent of the present kerosene subsidy bill; and 
(c) what are the other salient recommendations of the NCAER study report on 
the rationalization of kerosene subsidy? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (c) With a view to assessing the genuine demand 
requirement of kerosene in different States/UTs, in 
160 

[6 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
December 2004 the Government commissioned the first-ever comprehensive 
study of the subject through the National Council for Applied Economic 
Research (NCAER). NCAER have submitted their report in October 2005. 
A copy of the recommendations of the study is annexed as statement 
(See below). The recommendations of the study, inter-alia, include the 
following:— 
(i) The distribution of kerosene to households should follow a similar 
methodology as followed in the case of PDS of grains. All 
households possessing APL cards should purchase kerosene at the 
market price (as economic cost to the Government) and subsidized 
PDS kerosene should only be made available only to people with 
BPL, Annapurna, Antyodaya cards, etc. 
(ii) Taking out APL card holders from the purview of subsidies, PDS 
kerosene would amount to 41.2 per cent savings of current kerosene 
subsidy. If the leakage is controlled this saving can give enough 
scope to government to maintain the subsidized kerosene price for 
BPL families at a lower level. 
The report is under examination of the Government for taking an 
appropriate view on the recommendations. 
Statement 
Copy of the recommendations of the NCAER study report 
1. Although every State has two or three tiers of kerosene monitoring 
systems, this system is ineffective in controlling leakages and diversion of PDS 
kerosene. As a result, people are forced to buy kerosene from the market at 
more than double the PDS price. There is, therefore, an urgent need to 
overhaul the monitoring system. 
2. We think that by involving the panchayati raj institutions in villages and 
user committees in urban areas, the probl em could be solved to some extent. 
However, it is the State Governments' responsibility to make sure that the 
kerosene meant for house holds reaches to retailers in right time and right 
quantity. 
3. Although most of the BPL households are able to purchase their entire 
entitlement from PDS, some households are not able to purchase 
161 

RAJYA SAB HA [6 December, 2005] 
their entire entitlement from PDS. The reasons for this is poverty. It is 
difficult for a daily wage earner to purchase even five litres of kerosene at one 
time. Almost half of these households couldn't afford to buy their entire 
entitlement at one time and the rest use other, cheaper fuels, such as wood, 
crop waste, dung cake, etc. 
4. Government should look into the frequency of kerosene 
disbursement to BPL households and the same may be changed from 
monthly/fortnightly to weekly basis for BPL cardholders. This will help daily 
wage earners in taking their weekly entitlement. 
5. State specific duties are quite high in  some States, but his problem is 
partially solved by implementation of State level VAT. However, with the 
implementation of VAT, prices have co me down in the States where State 
level duties were high but have gone up where the State level taxes were low. 
6. There should not be any inter-and intra-State differential in kerosene 
prices. States may consider having uniform retail selling price of kerosene 
throughout the State. 
7. Different State Govern ments follows different criteria for making 
allocations of PDS kerosene to different types of card holders. Generally, 
allocation depends on whether a household has a LPG connection or not. 
However, we found that the kerosene requirement of different types of 
cardholders is higher than  their current level of consumption. The average 
current requirement of ru ral BPL card holders at the all-India level is 18 
percent more than their current level of consumption. Similarly, for APL and 
other card holders, the current requirement is higher by 13 and 24 per cent, 
respectively at the all-India level. In urban areas, the curr ent requirement of 
BPL, APL and other card-holders is more than their current level of 
consumption by 12, 7 and 18 percent, respectively. 
8. Current household kerosene demand (inclusive of unmet demand) is 
nearly 93 per cent of sale of PDS kerosene. With proper monitoring, 
plugging in leakages in PDS kerosene distribution and reallocation of PDS 
kerosene across States, current level of sale of PDS kerosene would satisfy 
unment kerosene demand. 
9. Kerosene demand is sensitive to price as far as heating (cooking and 
water heating) is concerned. Kerosene demand for lighting would 
162 

[6 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
not change with respect to a change in prices. Since, nearly 61 per cent 
consumption of kerosene is for lighting, there will not be much impact of-a 
price change on kerosene demand A one per cent increase in kerosene price 
would reduce kerosene demand for heating by 0.23 per cent and overall 
kerosene demand by 0.11 per cent. Thus, kerosene demand is relatively price 
inelastic. With increase in kerosene price, some rural households may shift 
to other non-commercial fuels, such as wood, crop waste, d ung cake, etc. In 
urban areas people would shift from kerosene to LPG. However, if the 
change in kerosene prices is gradual and not in two or three years, kerosene 
demand would not go down much. 
10. The distribution of kerosene to households, should follow a 
similar methodology as followed in the case of PDS of grains. All 
households possessing APL cards should purchase kerosene at the market 
price (as economic cost to the Government) and subsidized PDS kerosene should 
only be made available to people with BPL, Annapuma, Antyodaya cards, etc. 
only. 
11. PDS kerosene is supplied for fishing in some coastal States. Kerala 
provide a sizeable amount of kerosene to fishing community from their PDS 
allocation. Kerosene requirement for fishing may be supplied at non-PDS 
price. 
12. Taking out APL card holders from the purview of subsidies, PDS 
kerosene would amount ta-41.2 per cent savings of current kerosene subsidy. If the 
leakage is controlled this saving can give enough scope to Government to 
keep subsidized kerosene price for BPL families at lower level.

Rain Water Harvesting 
1504. SHRI T.T.V DHINAKARAN: W ill the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the salient features of the report "Master Plan for Artificial 
Recharge to Ground Water" prepared by the Cenral Ground Water Board; 
(b) the steps taken by Government to encourage rain water harvesting; 
and 
(c) whether Government propose to provide incentive to States like 
Tamil Nadu which are implementing rain water harvesting successfully? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) The Central Ground 
Water Board (CGWB) has prepared a report entitled "Master Plan for 
Artificial Recharge to Groundwater", which envisages recharge of 36453 
Million Cubic Metre volume of surplus monsoon run-off, through 
construction of 39.25 lakh artificial recharge and roof top rain water 
harvesting structures in the identified areas of 4.5 lakh Sq. Km..The report 
outlines broad framework about feasibility of these recharge structures in 
various parts of the country. The Master Plan is a conceptual document. 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2005] 
(b) 'Water' being a State subject, it is primarily the responsibility of the 
concenred State Government to take steps to encourage rain water harvesting. 
However, the following steps have been taken by the Union Government to 
encourage rain water harvesting:— 
(i) Circulation of Manual/Guidelines on Artificial Recharge of Ground 
Water to the States/Union Territories to enable them to formulate area 
specific artificial recharge schemes to check the declining trend of 
ground water levels. 
(ii) Central Ministries/Departments  of Railways, Defence, Posts, 
Telecommunications, Central Public Works Department and 
National Highways Authority of India have been requested to 
provide rooftop rain water harvesting structures in the buildings under 
their control. 
(iii) The CGWB has implemented a Central Sector Scheme on Study of 
Recharge to Ground Water in the country during the Ninth Plan 
under which 165 demonstrative recharge projects were taken up. 
(iv) Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) has issued directions to 
Group Housing Societies, Institutes, Hotels, Industries, Farm Houses, 
etc., in the notified areas of Delhi, Faridabad, Gurgaon and Ghaziabad 
and other areas of NCT Delhi where ground water table is below 8 
metres from ground surface, to adopt rain water harvesting system. 
(v) CGWB has provided technical guidance on rain water harvesting to 
around 2000 agencies, includin g State Government agencies, 
educational institutions, private entrepreneurs and individuals. 
(vi) CGWA has also produced a film on rain water harvesting in urban 
areas, rain water harvesting in rural areas, ground water pollution etc., 
for wide publicity among masses for awareness of rain water 
harvesting. Mass awareness programmes and training courses on 
rainwater harvesting and artificial recharge of ground water have 
been organised throughout the country involving Central/State 
Governments/NGOs/VOs/RWAs/Educational Institutions/Industries 
and Individuals. Rain Water 
186 

[6 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Harvesting campaign has been launched keeping in view the various 
target groups. Publicity through print media, telecasting of spots on 
the television, broadcasting meassages on radio, holding of 
seminars, workshops, conferences etc., have also been undertaken. 
(vii) The Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation, 
Government of India have amended Building Bye-laws, 1983, 
making provision for water harvesting through storihg of water run-
off including rain water in all new building on plots of 100 square 
metres and above in Delhi mandatory. Similarly, State Governments 
of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana, Rajasthan and 
Kerala have made rooftop rain  water harvesting mandatory in 
specified cases. 
(c) No, Sir. 
Storage of ground water 
1505. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Central Government have issued any directions to the 
State Governments to take necessary steps to preserve the ground water storage 
against its unlimited exploitation; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reaction of the States particularly State 
Governments of Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Punjab and Delhi; 
(c) whether Government are contemplating to introduce any special 
scheme to minimize the use of ground water; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the average rate of extraction of ground 
water for agriculture per day? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) and (b) The Union 
Ministry of Water Resources has circulated a Model Bill to all the States/ Union 
Territories to enable them to enact suitable legislation for regulation and control of 
ground water development. Most of the State Government 
187 

RAJYA SABHA [6 December, 2005] 
have reacted positively and are taking steps for enactment of legislation in this 
regard. As per information available, the States of Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Tamil 
Nadu, Goa, West Bengal and Union Territories of Pondicherry and 
Lakshadweep have enacted legislation for this purpose. The position in respect 
of Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Punjab and Delhi is given below:— 
(i) Maharashtra:— Maharashtra Ground Water Regulation Act has been 
drafted by the State Government who is processing it for enactment. 
(ii) Rajasthan:— Rajasthan Ground Water (Regulation) Bill, 1997 has 
been drafted by the State Governme nt who is evaluating the impact 
of similar legislation enacted in other States. 
(iii) Punjab:— The Punjab Ground Water (Control and Regulation) Act, 
1998 was prepared on the basis of Model Bill and was submitted to 
the Punjab State Water Reso urce Committee. However, the 
Committee observed that the draft is too harsh on users. The 
Committee decided after considering the report of the expert group 
to first control the demand, to make some corrective measures for 
optimum use of ground water and its augmentation. They also 
opined that Punjab being an irrigation State and dependant upon 
ground water, adoption of Model Bill is not in the larger interest of 
the farmers and suggested that a system of incentives is better. 
(iv) Delhi:— The State Government is in the process of changing the 
Delhi Water Board Act to accommodate concerns expressed in the 
Model Bill, draft of which has since been prepared and at consultation 
stage. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) Does not arise.

River linking projects 
1506. SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Committee appointed to study the linking of rivers in 
the country submitted its report and the period if any, fixed therefor; 
(b) whether there is any proposal to implement Pamba, Achancoil and 
Vaippar linking project and whether this project is against the interests of Kerala; 
and 
(c) the reaction of State Government of Kerala thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) Ministry of Water 
Resources has constituted a Committee of Environmentalists, Social 
Scientists and other Experts under the Chairmanship of Secretary, Ministry 
of Water Resources with a view to make the process of proceeding on 
Interlinking of Rivers (ILR) consultative. The role of Committee is advisory 
in nature and it is required to render its advice to the Government from time to 
time on various aspects of ILR viz. environmental and Socio-economic issue, 
Rehabilitation & Resettlement, additional studies that may be required, impact 
of proposed links and adoption of appropriate measures for optimum 
utilisation of transferred water. The Committee is not required to submit any 
report. 
(b) and (c) National Water Development Agency (NWDA) has 
prepared a feasibility report of transferring surplus water of Pamba and 
Achankovil situated in Kerala to Vai ppar river basin in Tamil Nadu. The 
Government of Kerala has some reservations on the studies done which have 
been clarified by NWDA. The Government of Kerala has forwarded a copy 
of the Resolution dated 6.8.2003 adopted unanimously by the Kerala 
Legislative Assembly urging the Central Government to give up the Pamba-
Achankovil-Vaippar Link Project completely.
