Water crisis forecast 
1507 SHRI ANAND SHARMA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the recent survey 
reports warning about drying of Aquifers in the coming years and forecasts of a 
severe water crisis in India; and 
(b) the steps proposed for management and conservation of ground water in 
the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) "Water" being a State subject, it is primarily the responsibility of the 
concerned State Governments to take steps for management and conservation 
of ground water in the country. However, following steps have been taken by 
the Union Government in this regard:— 
(i) Model Bill has been circulated to the States/Union Territories to 
enable them to enact suitable legislation for regulation and control 
of ground water development. Central Ground Water Authority 
(CGWA) has also notified specified critical areas for regulating 
drawl of ground water. 
(ii) Steps have been taken to adopt artificial recharge and rain water 
harvesting measures which include, circulation of Manual/ 
Guidelines on Artificial Recharge of Ground Water to States/ Union 
Territories, implementation of a Central Sector Scheme for Study of 
Recharge to Ground Water during the VIII & IX Five Year Plans. 
(iii) Steps have been taken for creation of mass awareness on water 
conservation by holding mass awareness and training programmes on rain 
water harvesting and artificial recharge of ground water. Water 
conservation campaigns launched keeping in view the various target 
groups like youth and children, women, farmers and villagers, etc., 
publicity done through mass media etc. 
190 

[6 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) The Ministry of Agriculture has implemented the National 
Watershed Development Project for Rainfed Areas (NWDPRA), 
whose impact evaluations have shown that watershed based 
interventions have led to increase in ground water recharge. Soil 
and water conservation works are also included under various 
activities of area development programmes, being undertaken by the 
Department of Land Resources. However, funds under the above 
programme are not exclusively allotted for checking declining ground 
water, which is a resultant activity of moisture conservation works 
undertaken for the development of watershed areas.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Question No. 202. Shri A. Vijayaraghavan. 
Defence framework agreement with various countries 
*202. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHVAN: W ill the Minister of DEFENCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether there are many attempts to have defence framework 
agreements with various countries for the last three years;

Statement 
(a) to (c) Agreements in the field of defence cooperation with various 
countries are entered into from time to time depending upon the level of 
bilateral relations with the country involved. In the last three years, 
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) Agreement on Defence Cooperation have 
been entered into by India with It aly, Poland, Armenia, United Arab 
Emirates.Seychelles, Tanzania, Singa pore, Czech Republic, Hungary Brazil 
and Uzbekistan. However, with a large number of countries, including Russia, 
France and U.K., India has defence co -operation arrangements arising out of 
agreements reached earlier. 
A statement showing the number of exercises conducted by our Armed Forces 
with foreign countries during the same period is annexed at Statement-I (See 
Below) 
Training of Armed Forces personnel of foreign countries in Indian defence 
training institutions and establishments is being undertaken to enhance defence 
cooperation with the countries concerned either under the Indian Technical and 
Economic Cooperation/Special Aid Programme of Ministry of External Affairs 
or on self-financing basis. Personnel from our Armed Forces also participate in 
various courses/training programmes offered by some foreign countries. 
Defence cooperation with any foreign country is formulated in conjunction with 
India's stated foreign and defence policy goals.

†*204. SHRIMATI SU SHMA SWARAJ: Will th e Minister of NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the quantum of electricity being generated from solar energy in India; 
(b) the places where solar energy plants have been set up, so far;

(d) the quantum of available solar energy in India, tapped so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI VILAS MUTTEMWAR): (a) to 
(d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) A total of 32 grid interactive solar photovoltaic power plants have been 
installed in the country with financial support from the Government. These 
plants, with aggregate capacity of 2.1 Megawatt, are estimated to generate about 
2.5 million units of electricity in a year. 
(b) The list of 32 grid interactive solar photovoltaic power plants is given at 
enclosed Statement-I (See below). 
(c) The unit cost of electricity from solar photovoltaic plants is very high 
compared to electricity generated from conventional sources and other 
renewable energy sources such as wind, small hydro and biomass. At present, 
solar photovoltaic systems are mainly  being used for decentralized niche 
applications such as lighting, telecommunication and small power requirements 
in remote areas. 
(d) India receives solar energy equivalent to over 5,000 trillion kWh per year, 
which is far more than the total energy requirement of the country. However, 
due to high initial cost of solar energy systems, so far around 12.8 lakh solar 
photovoltaic systems aggregating to about 82 Megawatt capacity have been 
installed in the country. In addition about 11 lakh square metre collector area has 
been installed for solar water heating applications, which is equivalent to about 
770 Megawatt capacity.

1515. SHRI SITARAM YECHURY: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state:

organisations has held pre-Hong Kong Ministerial consultations with the

(d) what is the response of Government to the issues raised by the 
stakeholders in these consultations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Towards evolving India's negotiating strategies and position in the 
negotiatiosn launched at Doha in 2001, the Government has been holding 
consultations with stakeholders from time to time, including a series of 
consultation workshops and seminars organized jointly with the United Nations 
Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) between June through 
Nobvember 2005 at New Delhi as a part of Government's preparations for the 
forthcoming Ministerial Meeting of the World Trade Organization at Hong 
Kong, China, on 13—18 December 2005. Open notices were issued to invite 
information and participation from nongovernmental organizations, farmes' 
associations, industry representatives, research institutions, economists, consumer 
organisations, and any other interested party.

RAJYA  SABHA [7 December, 2005] 
(c) and (d) The broad project theme has been "Strategies and Preparedness 
for Trade and Globalisation in India", focusing on key trade and trade policy 
issues affecting India, including, food security and rural livelihoods. The 
participants were unanimous in their view that during the on-going WTO 
negotiations on agriculture, protecting the interests of India's farmers should be 
India's most important negotiating objective. Government has assured the 
participants that the interests of farmers would be protected without any 
compromises during the negotiations in accordance with the Doha mandate to 
negotiate substantial reductions in trade-distorting domestic support, 
elimination of all forms of export subsidies by an early end-date, substantial 
improvemens in market access as well as through appropriate policy 
flexibilities to safeguard food and livelihood security concerns and to meet 
rural development needs. The participants also noted the livelihood concerns 
arising from the industrial sector negotiations, such as in the small scale industries, 
and sought enhanced market access in goods and services of export interest to 
India. The Government has assured the participants that appropriate 
flexibilities to address any concerns w ill be negotiated consistent with the 
domestic imperatives and the mandate for negotiations in industrial goods and 
servics. Technical inputs and detailed deliberations at these consultation 
workshops, including on issues relating to subsidies and countervailing measures 
and protecting India's biological diversity, have been found useful. Suggestions 
received in any stakeholder consultation are appropriately factored in India's 
negotiating strategy and positions after due consideration.

Views of intellectuals on India's strategy in WTO 
1526. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be plesed to state; 
(a) whether it is a fact that the feeling amongst intellectuals is that "The 
solidarity of the South, and not expedient issue-based coalitions with USA/ EU, 
must be the bedrock of our strategy in WTO"; and 
(b) how far we have been able to move towards its fulfilment and what steps 
Ministry of Commerce have taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) and (b) A few intellectuals 
feel that "the solidarity of the South, and not expedient issue-based coalitions 
with USA/EU, must be the bedrock of our strategy in WTO". India has 
engaged in the ongoing WTO negotiations to ensure that its core concerns 
and interests continue to be adequately addressed as negotiations proceed from 
one stage to the next. India's approach to the negotiations is dictated by its 
national interests. For ensuring that our negotiating objectives find due 
refelction in the negotiated outcome, India has formed issue-specific coalitions 
with developing countries. Wherever there are common interests on specific 
issues in the WTO, India has worked with developed countries also. 
India is a coordinator of the G-20, a developing country alliance, which is 
actively contributing to all aspects of the agriculture negotiations. India has also 
been a prominent founder member of the G-33, a group of 44 developing 
countries that emphasizes the need for special instruments, namely, the Special 
Products and the new Special Safeguard mechanism (SSM), to address their food 
and livelihood security and rural development needs of the developing countries. 
In the agriculture negotiations, India and Brazil representing the G-20 are members 
of the Five Interested Parties (Australia, Brazil, EC, India and US). Spearheaded by 
India, the G-33 has been making substantive contribution on the evolution of 
Special Products and the SSM. 
In the Services' area, a Small Group, (co-chaired by India and US), a group of 
developed and developing countries, has been formed to provide impetus to 
Services' negotiations. In the negotiations on non-agricultural products' market 
access (NAMA), Argentina, Brazil and India have proposed 
76 

[7 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
a formulation for reduction of tariffs, based on each WTO member's present bound tariff 
average. 
On one of the most important outstanding implementation issue relating to the relationship 
between the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD and TRIPS, India has been 
instrumental in forming a group of developing countries (Brazil, Cuba, Ecuador, Peru, 
Thailand, Venezuela, Zambia, Bolivia) for demanding that patent applicants should 
disclose the country and source of origin of any biological material or associated 
traditional knowledge used in their inventions, and the patent system should be 
supportive of the informed consent and benefit sharing arrangements that national laws may 
prescribe. Protection of intellectual property rights of private individuals should be 
supportive of the larger societal interests enshrined in the CBD. 
India has also been working closely with broad developing country goupings, such 
as the Africa Group, the Africa, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) countries, and the Least 
Developed Countries (LDCs) to promote our common interests in the WTO.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI MANIKRAO GAVIT): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The main demands and arguments of the Greater Cooch Behar People's 
Association are (i) Merger of erstwhile Cooch Behar State with West Bengal 
from 1.1.1950 is illegal and unconstitutional, (ii) Formation of Greater Cooch 
Behar State comprising the Cooch Behar, Jalpaiguri, Darjeeling, North and 
South Dinajpur, districts of West Bengal and undivided Goalpara district of 
Assam, (iii) Election to Legislative Assembly should not be held in Cooch Behar, 
since the merger of Cooch Behar in the State of West Bengal is illegal, (iv) 
Implement the promises made in the merger agreement between the Maharaja 
of Cooch Behar and the Government of India, and (v) Form a caretaker 
Ministry immediately for administration of Cooch Behar. 
(d) The Government has examined the demands. It appears that there is 
nothing illegal or unconstitutional in the Instrument of Accession or the Merger 
Agreement, signed by the Maharaja of Cooch Behar in accordance with the Indian 
Independence Act, 1947 read with the relevant provision of the Government of 
India Act, 1935. The merger of the State of Cooch Behar with West Bengal 
from 1.1.1950 under the States Merger (West Bengal) Order 1949 also appears 
to be legal and valid. Further, no other issue in the Merger Agreement remains 
unimplemented. However, the present dissatisfaction seems to emanate from the 
economic backwardness of the people of Cooch Behar. Union Government has 
requested the State Government to take measures to address the issue of 
economic backwardness of the area, both in the long term and in the short term.

(d) if so, the details thereof during the last one year; 
(e) whether it is also a fact that the police atrocities and custodial torture 
have not ebbed; slum-dwellers are kicked out of their hutments and tribal people 
are displaced; 
(f) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(g) the steps to be taken by Government to improve the situation in 
coordination with the State Governments especially in Andhra Pradesh? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SHRIPRAKASH JAISWAL). (a) to (g) Government lays great 
importance on protection of human rights and prevention of human rights 
violations in the country. The Central Government has issued advisories from 
time to time to all State Governments to avoid violation of human rights. The 
National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has also been issuing guidelines 
on various human rights to the State Governments for prevention of violation of 
human rights. "Human Rights" has been included as a subject in the training 
curriculum for policemen. Government has also issued guidelines to all the State 
Government and UT Administrations from time to time bringing out important 
aspects which the police should bear in mind while dealing with public. These 
include observance of a law, using method of persuassion, advice and warning 
before application of force, to be courteous and well mannered particularly 
while dealing with women and avoid committing abuse of their authority etc. As 
per reports received from the State Governments and UT Administrations by the 
NHRC, the number of deaths in police custody has declined from 183 in the year 
2002-2003 to 136 in the year 2004-2005. In view of the above situation, it cannot 
be stated that human rights situation in the country is grim. As regards 
displacement of slum dwellers and tribal people, these are matters coming under 
"Police" and "Public Order", which are State subjects listed in List II of the 
Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and it is for the State Governments to take 
appropriate action under the law, keeping in mind the human rights of the 
people affected.

Assistance to Earthquake victims of Gujarat and Uttaranchal 
1573. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the victims of the earthquake in Uttaranchal and 
Gujarat States are still suffering for want of financial and other assistance by Union 
Government; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor and steps taken to provide necessary help for 
their livelihood and life; and 
(c) by when the full and final assistance is expected to be provided? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI S. REGUPATHY): (a) to (c) The State Government concerned is the first 
responder to any natural calamity situation and is responsible for undertaking 
rescue and relief operations including distribution of relief on the ground. For 
this purpose, a Calamity Relief Funds (CRF) has been constituted for each 
State with an allocated amount, which is contributed by the Government of India 
and the State Government in the ratio of 3:1. A Committee under the Chairmanship 
of Chief Secretary is fully empowered to operate the CRF in accordance with the 
approved items and norms. 
If the calamity is of a severe nature, the Government of India supplements the 
efforts of the State Government by providing additional financial assistance 
from National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF), after following the laid down 
procedure. 
In addition to the provision of State CRF, the Government of India had in the 
wake of the earthquake of Chamoli in 1999 provided to the then Government 
of Uttar Pradesh, an amount of Rs. 16.68 crore from the National F und for 
Calamity Relief (NFCR) for relief operations during the year 1999-2000. 
Similarly, in the wake of the earthquake of January, 2001 in Gujarat, the 
Government of India had provided an amount of Rs. 1467.37 crore to the 
Government of Gujarat from the National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF) 
during the years 2000-2001 and 2001-2002. 
No request/memorandum of these State Governments for financial 
assistance in the wake of these earthquakes is pending with the Government of India.

†1588. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) and (b) The Central 
Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) is empowered to issue licences for inter-State 
trading of eletricity under Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003. The CERC is also 
empowered to revoke the licence in public interest under the circumstances specified 
under Section 19 of the Electricity Act, 2003. As per the Central Electricity 
Regulatory Commission (CERC) (Procedure Terms and Conditions for grant of Trading 
Licence and other related matters) Regulations, 2004 the trading licensees are required to furnish 
information in specified form to the CERC on quarterly basis, a copy of which is also to be 
furnished to the Regional Load Dispatch Centre (RLDC) and Regional Electricity Board (REB) 
or the Regional Power Committee (RPC), as the case may be. The licensees are also required 
to post the said information on their web sites. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
136 

[7 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
It was brought to the notice of the CERC that the licensees were not complying 
with the requirements of submission of inforamtion to the REB/ RPC and RLDC, and 
posting the same on the web sites. The CERC issued orders directing the licensees to 
comply with the requirement of the Regulation. The licensees have since submitted the 
compliance report to the CERC. 
(c) The Electricity Act, 2003 empowers the CERC to fix the trading margin in 
the inter-State trading of electricity, if considered necessary. The CERC has not yet 
fixed the trading margin for any trading licensee. The CERC in its oders dated 
24.6.2005, inter alia, required two trading licensees, namely, PTC India Ltd. 
and Adani Exports Limited to explain the reasons for high trading margin being 
charged by them. The said licensees have since submitted their explanation before the 
Commission. 
(d) and (e) Global Energy Ltd. (GEL) applied in March, 2004 to the CERC for 
grant of licence for inter-State trading in electricity. As the application made by 
GEL was still pending, the CERC as an interim measure and by virtue of powers 
conferred under sub-section (2) of the Section 94 of the Electricity Act, 2003 by its 
interim order dated 31.3.2004 directed that GEL could undertake sale and purchase of 
electricity involving inter-State transmission till 15.5.2004 or till dispoal of its main 
application for grant of licence for trading, whichever was earlier and at its own risk. 
This order was further extended up to 30.6.2004 and subsequently up to 15.9.2004 and 
finally up to 15.10.2004. The CERC has directed GEL, the prospective licencee, to file 
certain details vide its Oder dated 28.9.2004. However, GEL has filed petition before 
the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi against the order of the Commission dated 28.9.2004. 
The High Court by its order dated 26.10.2004 directed that "the interim licence granted to 
the petitioner be extended till the next date of hearing." This interim order now stands 
extended till further order. Thus, in terms of the High Court's order, M/s. Global Energy 
Limited can undertake trading in formal licence has been issued in its favour. Since the 
matter is sub judice, no further action is being taken.

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) to (c) No, Sir.

Measures to enable consumers to choose power suppliers of 
their choice 
1603. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering to set up task force to work out 
ways and means of allowing consumers to choose power suppliers of their 
choice and trapping the surplus power generating capacity of the captive 
power plants to meet the shortfalls; and 
(b) if so, what are the details with the time-schedule for submission of reports 
by the task forces and implementation of their recommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) No, Sir. The 
Electricity Act, 2003 already mandate s the State Electricity Regulatory 
Commissions to introduce open access in such phases and subject to such 
conditions as may be specified within one year of the Act coming into force. 
160 

[7 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The Act further provides that the State Commission shall, not later than five years 
from the date of commencement of the Electricity (Amendment) Act, 2003, i.e. from 
27th January, 2004, by regulations, provide such open access to all consumers who 
require a supply of electricity where the maximum power to be made available at 
any time exceeds one megawatt. 
Under sub-section (2) of Section 42 of the Act, e surcharge in addition to the 
charges for wheeling is to be levied by the respective State Commission on 
consumers switching to alternate supplies under open access. Such surcharge is 
to be utilized to meet the requirements of current level of cross subsidy within the 
area of supply of the distribution licensee. An additional surcharge may also be 
levied under sub-section (4) of Section 42 for meeting the fixed cost of the 
distribution licensee arising out of his obligation to supply in cases where consumers 
are allowed open access. 
The National Electricity Policy states that the amount of surcharge and additional 
surcharge levied from consumers who are permitted open access should not become 
so onerous that it eliminates competition that is intended to be fostered in 
generation and supply of power directly to consumers through the provision of 
open access. It further states that it is essential that the Surcharge be reduced 
progressively in step with the reduction of cross-subsidies as provided in Section 
42 (2) of the Electricity Act, 2003. 
The National Electricity Policy also states that a large number of captive and 
standby generating stations in India have surplus capacity that could be supplied to 
the grid continuously or during certain time periods. These plants offer a sizeable 
and potentially competitive capacity that could be harnessed for meeting demand 
for power. Grid inter-connectionsfor captive generators shall be facilitated as per 
Section 30 of the Act. This should be done on priority basis to enable captive 
generation to become available as distributed generation along the grid. 
The policy further envisages that appropriate commercial arrangements would 
need to be instituted between licensees and the captive generators for harnessing of 
spare capacity energy from captive power plants. The appropriate Regulatory 
Commission shall exercise regulatory oversight on such commercial 
arrangements between captive generators and licensees determine tariffs when a 
licensee is the off-taker of power from captive plant. 
(b) Does not arise.

1610. SHRIMATI JAYA BACHCHAN: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to

course; and *

choosing groups or sections of community which are considered vote banks by the 
political party in power in a State? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) and (b) At, present three 
States viz. Andhra Pradesh, Punjab and Tamil Nadu are giving free supply of power 
without any ceiling on consumption to certain categories of consumers like 
agriculture. 
in some other States, free supply of electricity is available to certain category of 
consumers only upto a very limited level of consumption or connected load. 
A statement indicating the States and expenditure involved on free supply of electricity as 
per available information is at Statement (See Below)

may grant subsidy from its budget to any class of consumers if it so desires in the tariff 
determined by the State Electricity Regulatory Commission.

from the consumers to make the power sector sustainable. The policy also provides that a 
minimum level of support may be required to consumers living below poverty line and 
consuming only up a specified level say 30 units/month. Tariff for such consumers should 
also be at least 50% of the cost of the average cost of supply.

Providing pure drinking water 
1623. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that despite more than Rs.40 thousand crore spent 
by the Centre for providing pure drinking water to the rural masses of the country 
so far, the problems of pure drinking water persists; 
(b) if so the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is fact that there are 2 lakh contaminated water sources in the 
country and 14 thousand resources are still lying neglected; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
(e) whether matter has been enquired into to fix responsibility in this 
regard; and 
(f) the measure taken by Government to ensure supply of pure drinking water 
to people? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA): (a) and (b) Rural drinking water 
supply is a State subject. Government of India provides financial and 
technical assistance in this endeavour to State through a Centrally sponsored 
scheme, namely Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP). As a 
result of the substantial investment made by the Central and State Government 
in rural drinking water supply sector, out of the 14,22,664 rural habitations 
included in the Comprehensive action plan (CAP)—1999 about 96.13% rural 
habitation in the country have been fully covered, and 3.55% partially covered, 
with safe drinking water supply with the stipulated norms. As on 1.4.2005, the 
number of not covered habitations was 4588. 
(c) and (d) As per the water quality survey ordered in March 2000 and as 
reported by State Governments, 2,16,968 rural habitations are affected 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [7 December, 2005] 
with different water quality problems, as on 31/3/2004. The State-wise details 
of water quality affected habitations as on 31/3/2004 is given in the Statement to 
this reply. (See below) 
(e) and (f) Contamination of ground water is mainly geogenic in nature and gets 
aggravated due to overexploitation for irrigation and other purpose. The quality of 
drinking water of various sources is periodically monitored by the district water 
quality testing laboratories with reference to the water quality standards laid down 
by the Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission (RGNDWM) as per IS: 
10500 standard. 5% of ARWSP funds released to the States are earmarked for 
sustainability of drinking water sources, which also include 
improvement/revival of traditional sources. 15% of ARWSP funds released to 
States are earmarked for tackling water quality problems. For tackling water 
quality problems due to chemical contamination, a Sub-Mission programme was 
introduced in 1992-93 under ARWSP with funding pattern of 75:25 between 
the centre and States. With effect form 1/4/1998, the State Governments have 
been delegated powers to sanction projects under the Sub-Mission programme 
for which funds earmarked for water quality are to be utilized. 
Following water quality tackling measures were taken up by the State/ 
Central/Governments under the Sub-Mission Programme:— 
• Setting up the de-fluoridation plants, de-salination plants, arsenic 
removal plants for existing ground water schemes, treatment and 
filtration plants. 
• Providing Community de-fluoridation plants and domestic level filters. 
• Aeration for treatment of iron contaminated water. 
• Marking of safe and unsafe sources and social mobilization for usage of safe 
sources for drinking and cooking purposes. 
• Single and multi- village piped water schemes form alternative distant ground 
water/surface source. 
The State have also proposed that in future they would adopt an integrated approach 
to cover quality affected habitations by utilizing treatment units/ domestic filters, 
rooftop rainwater harvesting structures, piped water schemes and recharging/ 
strengthening of existing safe source and watershed based activities.  A 
community based rural drinking water 
186

monitoring and surveillance programme has also been pilot-tested in four districts 
of the country for scaling up throughout the country. 
A Model Bill to "Regulate and Control the Development and Management of 
Groundwater" has been prepared by Ministry of Water Resources and circulated 
to all the State Governments for enactment. 
It has been decided to cover all the remaining uncovered habitations of CAP-
1999, and address slippage and water quality problems under Bharat Nirman 
Programme in a period of four years (2005-09).

THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): (a) The

Indian textile items have witnessed a growth of 27.00% and 10.8% respectively. Even 
DGCI&S data for the period April-August, 2005 has shown a growth rate of 5.2% over 
the corresponding period of previous year. These markets account for 60% of Indian Textile 
Exports. The performance of India textile exporters compared to China is not that 
satisfactory due to the cost disadvantages on account of various market driven

GOVERNMENT BILLS (Cont.) 
The National Tax Tribunal Bill, 2005 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI HANSRAJ 
BHARDWAJ): Sir, I beg to move: 
'That the Bill to provide for the adjudication by the National Tax Tribunal of 
disputes with respect to levy, assessment, collection and 
enforcement of direct taxes and also to provide for the adjudication by that 
Tribunal of disputes with respect to the determination of the rates of duties 
of customs and central excise on goods and the valuation of goods for 
the purposes of assessment of such duties as well as in matters relating to 
levy of tax on service, in pursuance of article 323 B of the Constitution and 
for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto, as passed by Lok 
Sabha, be taken into consideration." 
Sir, the National Tax Tribunal Bill, 2005, aims at establishing National Tax 
Tribunal which will have jurisdiction to deal with disputes concerning both direct 
and indirect tax laws as is indicated in the long title of the Bill. 
Sir, as you are aware, this Bill was conceived by the earlier Government, that is, 
the NDA Government, and We are continuing with this. This Bill was passed 
by the Lok Sabha unanimously. 
Sir, the main objective behind setting up of this Tribunal is to speed up disposal 
of cases relating to direct and indirect tax matters. Apart from achieving the 
purpose of speedy disposal of tax matter, the setting up of, National Tax Tribunal 
will introduce an all-lndia perspective in the matter of interpretation of tax laws, 
since it will have a nationwide jurisdiction. It may also be noted that there are, 
at present, 21 High Courts. Many a 
259 

RAJYASABHA [7 December. 2005] 
times, decisions of the High Courts vary from each other, which create 
uncertainty, delays and problems in the administration of tax matters. Then, 
sometimes, there are conflict of decisions also. 
Sir, the National Tax Tribunal will hear appeals from order passed by 
Income-Tax Appellate Tribunal and Customs, Excise and Service Tax 
Appellate Tribunal on a substantial question of law. Presently, an appeal from 
these Tribunals on a substantial question of law lies to the High Court. After 
enactment of National Tax Tribunal Act, all cases pertaining to direct and indirect 
taxes pending before High Courts shall stand transferred to the National Tax 
Tribunal from such date as may be notified by the Central Government. 
Sir, the Tribunal shall consist of a Chairperson and such number of 
members as the Central Government deems fit. As mentioned in the financial 
memorandum, to begin with, it is considered necessary to have at least 15 
benches for direct tax matters and 10 benches for indirect tax matters so that 
cases, which shall stand transferred from the High Courts, may be disposed of 
quickly. 
The Chairperson of the Tribunal shall be a person who has been a Judge 
of the Supreme Court or the Chief Justice of a High Court. A person to be 
appointed as a Member should be one who is or has been or is eligible to be 
a Judge of a High Court or a person who is or has been a Member of the 
Income-Tax Appellate Tribunal or of the Central Excise, Customs and Service 
Tax Appellate Tribunal for, at least, seven years. Thus, the Tribunal will have 
Chairperson and Members having judicial and quasi-udicial experience, and as 
such it will be a specialist body exclusively devoted,to the tax matters. 
Sir, the Chairperson and Members shall be appointed by the Central 
Government on the recommendations of a Selection Committee consisting of the 
Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court nominated by Mm, 
Secretary in the Ministry of Law and Justice and Secretary in the Ministry of 
Finance, Department of Revenue. 
Sir, the litigation arising under the tax laws need a special skill to deal with 
the same. 
Therefore, keeping that necessity in view, the present Bill was introduced in the 
Lok Sabha, and I hope the Bill, as passed by the Lok Sabha, will receive the 
wholehearted support of this House also.

Demand to set up low temperature thermal desalination system 
plants in coastal areas of Andhra Pradesh for Conversion of Sea 
Water into potable water 
DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, in order to solve the 
problem of drinking water in coastal areas of the country, the Government have 
decided to set up desalination plants in various coastal areas and announced 
if in the current financial year's Budget. The proposed desalination plants 
will incur heavy expenditure. Recently, in reply to a question in the House, it 
was informed by Minister of State of the Department of Ocean Development that 
the National Institute of Ocean Technology has developed a Low Temperature 
thermal Desalination System (LTTDS) technology for conversion of seawater 
into potable water. Through this process, fresh water is produced by flashing 
warm surface seawater under low vacuum conditions and condensing the 
vapour, using cold deep seawater. The water quality is found to be excellent and 
cost of conversion works out to be around 25 paise per litre, which is very cheap. 
The cost is expected to come down further once higher capacity desalination 
plant is commissioned and run over a long period. The institute has set up a LTTDS 
plant with a capacity Of one lakh litres per day at Kavaratti in Lakshadweep. 
Since the coastal areas of my home State, Andhra Pradesh, are facing acute 
shortage of potable water, setting up of cheap LTTDS technology based 
desalination plants to such areas will give the desired relief to the people of 
these areas. Hence, I demand from the Government to set up LTTDS 
desalination plants at conspicuous places in the coastal are as of Andhra 
Pradesh to give the much*desired relief to the people of these areas on 
priority: basis. Thank you.

Demand for comprehensive action plan for effective prevention 
and control of Japanese encephalitis in Karnataka and other 
parts of the Country 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karnataka): Sir, Japanese Encephalitist is a 
seasonal and epidemic-prone disease spread by mosquitoes. It generally 
spreads in the rainy season, which is most suitable for mosquito breeding. This 
dreaded diseases takes a heavy toll particularly of the children. This year, 
Gorakhpur and adjoining areas of Eastern Uttar Pradesh, were in the grip of Japanese 
Encephalitis where there were 1387 confirmed deaths. This dreaded disease also 
affects many areas of my home State Karnataka. From the year 2002 to 
November, 2005, there were 617 cases of Japanese Encephalitis in Karnataka 
resulting in 36 deaths. During the same period, in 15 States of the country, 
11361 cases of Japanese Encephalitis were registered and 3079 deaths were 
caused. This vector-borne disease spreads a panic in the areas prone to it. It has to 
be controlled through preventive measures like vaccination, destruction of 
mosquitoes, laboratories for early detection and proper medical treatment in the 
disease-prone areas and more so in the tribal and village areas and slums and J J 
clusters in urban areas. 
I, therefore, demand from the Central Government to pay special attention towards 
eradication of Japanese Encephalitis from every parts of the country, including 
Karnataka. For this, vaccination should be undertaken in a big way by 
manufacturing it in the country or by importing it from Japan or elsewhere. For 
destroying mosquitoes, prescribed pesticides be sprinkled and fogging of effected 
areas be undertaken frequently. Now, a variety offish, which eats the larva of 
mosquitoes, be made available for the ponds and such stretches in the 
villages. Mosquito nets should be provided in the villages and tribal areas. 
Laboratories be established and medicines be made available to the States. 
States should be provided adequate funds to develop infrastructure to fight the 
menace of Japanese Encephalitis. Thank you.

DISCUSSION ON THE STATEMENT MADE BY MINISTER 
WTO Negotiations at its Sixth Ministerial Conference at Hong Kong 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL 
NATH): Sir, the Commerce and Trade Ministers of 148 WTO member 
countries are scheduled to meet at Hong Kong from 13-18 December, 
2005 to discuss and negotiate on the Doha work programme (also called 
the Doha Development Agenda) and July Framework Agreement of 2004. 
[MR CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
Members of the House would recall that I had made a statement in this 
House in August, 2004 after the framework agreement was negotiated. 
Somce then, there have been constant negotiations at the official as well 
as at ministerial levels India has been proactive in its participation in the 
negotiations in the WTO. India has participated in various formal and informal 
meetings not only for highlighting our developmental concerns, but also 
submitted a series of proposals on various issues. The proposals submitted 
are on issues of concern to India and also other developing countries. 
India is a member of various coalitions and groups with common interest 
in issues under negotiations. India is a member of the G-20, which has been 
at the forefront to bring about a more equitable order in agriculture. India is 
also a member of G-33, a group of 44 developing countries that focuses on 
special and differential treatment for developing countries to address their 
food security livelihood security and rural developmental needs. India has 
been closely workly with important groupings, such as Africa Group, LDCs 
an ACP (Africa, Caribean and Pacific) countries. I have attended meetings 
of the ACP Group and the G-90, to coordinate our positions in the common 
interest of development countrues. Only last week, I attended the meeting 
of the G-90 Ministers at Brussels and and a meeting of G-4 at Geneva. 
In non-agricultural market access negotiations, India has cosponsored 
a proposal with Brazil an Argantina, and also co-authored with 8 other 
developing countries, namely Argentina, Brazil, sough Africa, Pakistan, 
Namibia, Indonesia, Philippines and Venezueula, a paper that highlights 
the need for a 'development focus' in all aspects of the Doha negotiations. 
India, along with a number of developing countries including, the group 
of Mega-Diverse countries, has sought amendment in the TRIPS

Agreement for including "disclos ure requirements" in the patents 
applications to prevent piracy of biological material, and misappropriation of 
traditional knowledge. Bio-piracy and misappropriation seriously affects the 
develpmental benefits, environmental Benefits, and the economic benefits 
of the poor and under-privieged community, who are holders of biological 
material and associated Traditional knowledge. We want that granting of 
patents on products out of the biological material and processes, based on 
Traditonal knowledge, should not over look the interests if the holders of 
such biological material and knowledge as that undermines the prospects 
of conservation and sustainable use of genetic resources and prospects 
of conservation and sustainable use of genetic resources and 
associated Traditional Knowledge as that undermines the prospects of 
conservation and sustainable use of genetic resources and assoicated 
Traditional Knowledge. Disclosure of the source and country of origin of the 
biological resources and traditional knowledge in the patent applications, 
along with prior informed consent and equitable benefit sharing, would be a 
fair and equitable way to address the shortcomings in the TRIPS 
Agreement. 
On the Singapore issues, India is a member of the core group which 
was instrumental in ensuring that the issures of investment, competition 
policy and transparency in government procurement were dropped from 
the potentially has a developmental dimension. 
In the Services negotiations, India co-chairs with US, a core group of 14 
countries which was set up to give momentum to the Service negotiations 
which are of importance to India considering that 52 per cent of India's 
GDP comes from the services sector. 
For the Doha negotiations, extensive preparatory measures have been 
undertaken to finalise India's position on various issues in the WTO-
positions that reflect both the domestic, consensus on issues and that 
which best protect our interest. The domestic preparatory process has 
included wide ranging inter-ministerial and inter- departmental discussions. 
Inter- departmental delegations have been paricipating in the actual 
negotiations at Geneva as well as at other centres. Discussions have 
been conducted with the State Government though regular information 
sharing and infomation gather meetings. Workshops and semiars have 
been held in various cities in India on the ongoing negotiations. 
For analytical back up, various academic and research institutions were 
identified early on and asked to carry out research studies. This has helped 
create Centres of excellence on specific WTO issues. The inputs from the 
studies conducts by these institutions and reports received from various 
other organisations have been used for formulating India's proposals. We 
297 

RAJYASABHA [7 December, 2005] 
have also held wide stakeholder consultations with business operatives, farmer groups, 
industry associations and civil society. These have been held together with a large 
number of organisations/NGOs working in the field on these issues. These 
meetings have been informative as well as educative. 
Finally, we have ensured that the Parliament and all parties are fully kept 
informed about these negotiations. I have met my colleagues from different potical 
parties to brief them, about the issues invloved in the negotiations. 
Coming to India's position on the issues under negotiations, the most 
important sector is agriculture. As far as India is concerned, agriculture is not 
commerce for a vast majority of Indian farmers, it is a matter of livelihood for millions 
of India and their interests are to be fully protected. Members are aware that 
agriculture is the most structurally imbalanced among all the trading sectors, 
primarily, due to the huge subsidies given to the farmers/agri business in the 
developed world. In this round, it has been agreed that all export subsidies in 
agriculture would be eliminated; only the end date is to the negotiated. India's 
priority is to obtain substantial reduction of trade and distoring subsidies and 
domestic support by the developed countries. The G-20 has put forward its 
position inter alia indicating that the overall trade distorting support is reduced 
by 83 per cent highlighting the importance of agriculture. The G-20 has also 
stated that developed countries should cut their tariff by at least 64 per cent of 
their bound rates on average, and that developing countries should not have 
to cut more than two thirds of what the developed countries do. In addition, 
appropriate provisions to safeguard food security, livelihood security and 
rural development needs would be obtained through designation of an 
appropriate number of special products and a simple special safeguard 
mechanism which would guard against import surges and price falls in agriculture 
commodities. We have also stated categorically that developing countries like 
India, which allocates almost all its domestic subsidies to subsistence and 
resource poor farmers, should not be called upon to make any reduction in their 
de minimis entitlements. 
As far as non-agricultural goods are concerned there is a broad 
consensus on the application of Swi ss formula, only its structure and 
flexibilities for developing countries are yet to be finally negotiated. India has 
repeatedly stressed that as per the July framework agreement, developing 
countries would offer less than full reciprocity in reduction commitments and 
that any formula finally negotiated must respect this. Developed countries 
have yet to respond. While undertaking tariff cuts, we have also provided for 
adequate flexibilities to protect small scale 
298 

[7 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
4.00 P.M. 
industries, infant industries and sensitive sectors. The issue of binding all non-
agricultural tariff lines is also under negotiation. 
India has a strong comparative advantage in services. It is this strength and 
global competitiveness that has guided our stance in the GATS negotiations 
at the WTO. Our core objectives in this area are liberalisation of Mode 1 (Cross 
Border Supply) and Mode 4 (Movement of Natural persons) and disciplining of 
domestic regulations, which act as barries to effective market access for service 
providers from India. 
In making our conditional offers we have not gone beyond the level of 
autonomous liberalisation in any sector, while expanding sectoral and modal 
coverage as compared to our Uruguay Round commitments. The efforts from the 
developed countries have so far been disappointing. However, the negotiations on this 
are expected to continue well into the year 2006 and final results would be 
available only at the end of 2006. 
India has been at the forefront of recognition of the principles of "access to 
medicines for all at affordable prices" and was instrumental in getting all the 
WTO members to agree to introduce certain flexibilities agreed in the August 
2003 decision are fully preserved in the eventual amendment to the TRIPS 
agreement so that the developed goals of countries which have inadequate or no 
manufacturing capacity are not undermined. 
In the negotiations on trade and environment, we want to address the 
environmental concerns in a manner that we retain appropriate national policy 
space without undermining our common global responsibilities. We also want that 
the negotiations under trade and environment bring out the environmental 
benefits, the developmental benefits and the economic benefits in a "win-win-
win" manner, rather than only an increase in market access. 
In the negotiations on WTO rules such as on anti-dumping, subsidies and 
countervailing measures including fisheries subsidies, while India is not seeking 
to straicacket disciplines to an extent that WTO Members cannot check unfair 
trade practice, India seeks strengthenig of disciplines consistent with the Doha 
mandate in order to limit the unwarranted use of these measures, particularly 
against the exports from developing countries, including India. 
299 

RAJYASABHA [7 December, 2005] 
On trade facilitation, the last 'Singapore issue' still remaining on the 
Doha agenda, the negotiation's have been far less contentious. It potentially 
has a strong development dimension. So far, a large number of proposals 
have been made on issues concerning import and export procedures. 
India is actively participating in the negotiations and has submitted proposals 
for an effective cooperation mechanism between the customs 
administrations of the WTO Members. Technical assistance and capacity 
building in developing countries is another area where Ministers are focusing 
their energies. 
On developmental issues, developing countries have put forth several 
constructive proposals. These include the implementation issues which 
are of considerable significance to us. We are seeking substantive progress 
on these issues both in the run up to and at Hong Kong. It is important 
that the WTO Members agree on an S&D package for the Least Developed 
Countries as well as ensure that effective special and differential treatment 
is provided for developing countries in all areas of the negotiations. India 
is also looking to provide additional market access to the products of the 
Least Developed Countries. 
One other issue that has to be meaningfully addressed in this Round to 
make it a truly development Round is the concern regarding preference 
erosion. There are several developing countries that are dependant on a 
majority of their exports to the developed markets through systems, of 
unilateral preferential tariffs. The reduction in tariffs following from this Round 
of negotiations will adversely impact the preference margins that these 
countries now enjoy thereby constricting their exports. This issue has to 
be handled carefully without in anyway slowing down the multilateral 
liberalisation process. 
The draft ministerial text has been released in the WTO. It would be 
seen that there are wide divergence on a large number of issues, especially 
in agriculture and other goods. Our efforts would be to try and seek 
convergence on many of the outstanding issues. It is believed that full 
modalities in agriculture and other goods would not be possible in Hong 
Kong and that there may be a need for another ministerial meeting earlier 
next year to complete this stage of the negotiations. Hong Kong is, 
300 

[7 December, 2005] RAJYASABHA 
therefore, a staging post to bringing about greater convergence so that full 
modalities could be achieved in 2006. India looks forward to the successful 
completion of the Doha Development Round by the end 2006.

*221. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the roof of an abandon ed CCL, Colliery near Hazaribag 
collapsed on 28 th/29th September, 2005 leading to  the death of a number of 
persons engaged in illegal mining there; 
(b) if so, the number of the persons who lost their lives in the mishap; 
(c) whether the matter has been investigated as to the role of unauthorized 
contractors/officials of the CCL, and others in the illegal mining which led to 
the mishap; and 
(d) if so, the findings thereof and the action taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYAN RAO): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of 
the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes Sir, a portion of mine roof collapsed at Section-I quarry of 
Rajrappa Project of Central Coalfiel ds Ltd. near Hazaribagh, Jharkhand 
while illegal mining was being done on 29.9.2005. The Officer Incharge of 
Rajrappa Police Station in his report dated 29.9.2005 has mentioned that two 
bodies were recovered from the accident site. 
(c) and (d) The police has registered a case vide Rajrappa Police outpost 
(Police Station, Ramgarh), case No. 399/05 dated 29.9.05 under sections 
286,287,338,379,304(A) of the Indian Penal Code and Section 30(ii) of the 
Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 and the matter is under enquiry by 
the police.

*230. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will th e Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD

THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) to  (c) A Statement is laid on the

Statement 
(a) Reliable statistics regarding the road accidents as well as the vehicle 
population for the world is not available in any source known to the 
Government. While the number of accide nts as reported by the States and 
UTs in the country is known, the same is not known for the entire world. 
Similarly, while the number of registered vehicles in the country is being 
maintained by the Government, the same is not available for the world as a 
whole. Further, inter-country compar ison of accidents and fatalities is also 
difficult because of different road tra ffic conditions and different practices 
followed by the countries in compiling such statistics. 
(b) Road accidents are caused by a number of factors such as driver's 
fault, mechanical defects in the vehicles, fault of pedestrians, bad arods, bad 
weather etc.

(c) Enforcement of safety-related regulations comes under the purview of 
the State Governments. Some of the other important preventive steps 
taken/being taken by the Central Government to check the road accidents 
besides highway design are as under: 
• Awareness campaigns on road safety through audio-visual/print 
media, NGOs, Training to Drivers, etc. 
• Widening and improvements of National Highways with divided 
carriageways. 
• Improvement of junctions/intersections. 
• Rectification of deficient road geometry of National Highways. 
• Provision of bypasses and flyovers/grade separators. 
• Improvement in road markings/signs. 
• Provision of safety barriers and guard rails at hazardous locations. 
As regards post-accidents measures, evacuation of accidents victims to the 
nearest medical aid centre and removal of accident affected vehicles is the 
primary responsibility of the concerned State/UT Governments except for the 
stretches entrusted to NHAI. However, this Ministry provides Cranes and 
Ambulances under National Highway Accident Relief Service Scheme to 
States/UTs/Non Governmental Organisations for clearing accident sites and 
evacuating accident victims to the nearest medical aid centre. For the 
stretches with NHAI under 'Operation and Maintenance Contract' an 
ambulance, patrol vehicle and a crane ar e provided on an average stretch of 
50 Kms. 
Strengthening of road safety measures is a continuous and ongoing 
exercise.

underground coal gasification projects. The joint venture of CIL and ONGC

An incident of sudden slide of O.B. occurred on 25th August, 2001 when

partially damaged, which was taken out for repair on the 3rd day of the

crores. This shovel is not new and this shovel was commissioned on

consisting of senior officers. While attributing the presence of hidden slip, 
which could not be noticed during regular mine inspection, as the root cause 
responsible for the accident, the commi ttee found the shif t incharge and 
Section Manager of the coal company responsible for failing of their duties 
and not taking necessary precautions. They were issued warning letters. 
The shovel was recommissioned on 1 st  January, 2003 after necessary 
repairs. The total cost of repairs including parts was Rs. 2.89 crores. 
(c) As reported by Coal India Limited it is not a fact that shovel machine 
worth Rs. 8 crores belonging to Khadia Project was damaged completely in 
an accident last year. However, on 23rd October, 2004, at about 8.30 PM, the 
BE-195 10 Cubic Metre Shovel having CIL No. EXC-1696, named Vikas 
was partially damaged during the idle hours, due to sudden slide of Dragline 
dump. The machine was kept at safe distance. In spite of all precautions 
taken as stipulated by Department of Mines and other agencies

approximately (2.84% of the cost of the shovel), to bring the shovel 
in state of full fledged operation. 
(iii) Though the shovel was out of op eration for three and half months, 
still the coal production (in which the shovel was deployed) for the 
financial year 2004-05 was Rs. 39.33 lakhs tonnes against the 
targeted production of 38 lakhs tonnes, which is highest ever since

Copy of the press note issued by Ministry of Commerce and Industry

PRESS NOTE NO. 5 (2005 SERIES) 
Subject:   Enhancement of the Foreign Direct Investment ceiling from 49th 
per cent to 74 per cent in the Telecom sector. 
1. In pursuance of the Government's commitment to liberalise the FDI 
regime, it has been decided to enhance the Foreing Direct Investment ceiling 
from 49 per cent to 74 per cent in certa in telecom services [such as Basic, 
Cellular, Unified Access Services, National/International long Distance, V-
Sat, Public Mobile Radio Trunked Services (PMRTS), Global Mobile 
Personal Communications Services (GMPCS) and other value added 
services], subject to the following conditions:— 
A. The total composite foreign holding including hut not limited to 
investments by Foreign Institutional Investors (Flls), Non-Resident 
Indians (NRIs), Foreign Currenc y Convertible Bonds (FCCBs), 
American Depository Receipts (ADRs), Global Depository Receipts 
(GDRs), convertible preference shares, proportionate foreign 
86 

[8 December, 2005] RAJYASABHA 
investment in Indian promoters/investment companies including 
their holding companies, etc., here inafter referred as FDI, will not 
exceed 74 per cent. Thus, 74 per cent foreing investment can be 
made directly or indirectly in the operating company or through a 
holding company. Hence, the rema ining 26 per cent will be owned 
by resident Indian citizens or an Indian Company (i.e. Foreign 
Direct Investment does not exceed  49 per cent and the management 
is with the Indian owners). It is clarified that proportionate foreign 
component of such as Indian Company will also be counted towards 
the ceiling of 74%. However, foreign component in the total 
holding of Indian public sector banks and Indian public sector 
financial institutions will be treated as 'Indian' holding. The licensee 
will be required to disclose the status of such foreign holding and 
certify that the foreign investment is within the ceiling of 74% on a 
half yearly basis. 
B. The majority Directors on th e Board including Chairman, Managing 
Director and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) shall be resident Indian 
citizens, enforced through licen ce agreement. The appointment 
to these positions from among resi dent Indian citizens shall be 
made in consultation with serious Indian investors. Serious investor 
has been defined below inpara G(ii). 
C. The share Holder Agreements (S HA) shall specifically incorporate 
the condition that majority directors on the Board including 
Chairman, Managing Director and CEO shall be resident Indian 
citizens and shall also envisage the conditions of adherence to 
Licence Agreement. 
D. FDI upto 49 per cent will continue to be on automatic route. Foreign 
Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) approval shall be required for 
FDI in the licensee company/In dian promoters/investment 
companies including their holding companies if it has a bearing 
on the overall ceiling of 74 per cent. While approving the 
investment 
proposals, FIPB shall take note that investment is not coming 
from unfriendly countries. 
E. The investment approval by FIPB shall envisage the conditionality 
that Company would adhere to licence Agreement. 
F. FDI shall be subject to laws of India and not the laws of the foreign 
country/countries.

Expert Group on 'Estimation of Proportion and Number of Poor' (Lakdawala

submitted its Report to the Planning Commission in July, 1993. A full 
Planning Commission meeting chaired by the Prime Minister in March, 1997 
accepted the recommendations of the Expert

goods and services anchored on a norm of per capita daily calorie 
requirement of 2400 kcal in rural areas. The prescribed per capita 
consumption expenditure limit in rural areas is then updated using State-
specific cost of living indices for Ag ricultural Labourers (CPIAL) for rural 
areas. The national poverty line at 1999-2000 prices is Rs. 327.56 per capita 
per month in rural areas. 
(e) The percentage of persons living below the poverty line in the country 
was 26.10 during 1999-2000, according to the 55th round of NSS Household 
Consumer Expenditure Survey. The co rresponding figures are 27.09 and 
23.62 for rural and urban areas respectively. The Planning Commission does 
not estimate the number of families living below poverty line.

recognized that gainful employment can only come from robust growth of 
economy especially in labour using sectors.

Plan, since growth in this sector is likely to lead to the widest spread 
of benefits especially to the rural poor.

those sectors, which are most lik ely to create gainful employment 
opportunities and deal with the policy constraints, which discourage 
growth of employment. Particular attention must be paid^to the 
policy environment influencing a wide range of sectors,

(c) As per Section 358 of Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, a shipping

(i) on or near the coasts of Indian, any ship is lost, abandoned, stranded

damage to any other ship; 
(iii) any loss of life ensues by reason of any casualty happening to or on 
board any ship on or near the coasts of India; 
(iv) in any place, any such loss, abandonment, stranding, material 
damage or casualty as above mentioned occurs to or on board any 
Indian ship, and any competept witness thereof is found in India; 
(v) any Indian ship is lost or is supposed to have been lost and any 
evidence is obtainable in India as to the circumstances under which 
she proceeded to sea or was heard of; 
In all such cases, the appointed officer makes the preliminary inquiry into 
the casaulty. However, no investigati on is conducted under the Merchant 
Shipping Act, 1958 in casualities falling out side the purview of section 358
